summary: The deployment of Live Facial Recognition (LFR) surveillance in the United Kingdom is substantially increasing in publicly accessible places. Both public and private bodies have incorporated this enhanced level of biometric surveillance within their public space overwatch strategies. This thesis adopts a socio-legal approach to examining the relationship between the increasing prevalence of LFR and the regulation that authorises and constrains its use in public spaces. In analysing the current doctrinal frameworks regulating LFR surveillance by police and private bodies, this thesis demonstrates how subtle differences in the Data Protection Act (DPA) 2018, the bedrock of LFR regulation, assist in allowing private bodies to target a broader category of individuals. summary: Temperament has been defined as individual constitutionally-based differences in self-regulation and reactivity that are impacted by maturation and environment (Rothbart & Derryberry, 1981). summary: The South Asian region, a quarter of the world’s population, experienced a 3.0% rise in the incidence of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) from 2010 to 2021. title: The violent disconnection: the logic of protest violence in contemporary Latin America
summary: Scholars have extensively debated the causes of recent anti-government protests in Global South democracies. However, little attention has been given to explaining why and how some of these protests became more violent than others despite occurring under relatively similar circumstances. In contemporary Latin America, most countries have experienced mass anti-government protests, but only a few escalated into highly destructive, nationwide, and prolonged street violence. This puzzle set the central question of this PhD research: How can we explain variation in the intensity of protest violence in low-middle quality democracies? title: Labour, protest and the Tishreen uprising: popular politics in Iraq after Saddam
summary: Based on interviews and fieldwork between 2022-2025, this thesis is about anti-sectarian popular struggles in Iraq from the US-led invasion of 2003 to the Tishreen Uprising of 2019. The thesis shows how nearly two decades of labour mobilization and popular protest set the stage for the largest popular uprising since the fall of Saddam which sought to overturn the corrupt ethno-sectarian regime established under foreign occupation. Using a Gramscian framework, it argues that popular struggles culminating with Tishreen did not achieve their aims due in part to their organizational fragmentation and ideological underdevelopment.

summary: There is a critical nursing shortage worldwide and newly licensed registered nurses (NLRN) are needed to fill this gap. Approximately one out of five NLRN (30,000) will leave the nursing field after the first year, and another 1/3 (20,000) will leave within two years. title: Are we the people? Democratic municipalism in two European cities, in the approach to power and thereafter 2011-2024
summary: This thesis examines the theory and practice of democratic (“new”) municipalism, as it has been expressed in Madrid, Spain and Zagreb, Croatia. In theory, municipalism aims to reclaim popular control over key dimensions of everyday urban life — from housing and infrastructure to public services — through a unique hybridization of participatory policy formation with conventionally electoral contestation. While widely celebrated in activist and scholarly discourse, however, the ability of municipalist formations to produce real-world outcomes consonant with their aims has varied sharply from place to place, and the tradition’s present vitality and capacity to produce new liberatory openings is in question. title: SCORING MOTIVATIONAL ASSESSMENTS WITH FREE RESPONSES VIA TRANSFORMERS
summary: Student motivation is a well-established predictor of academic engagement and achievement. Despite its importance, motivation is difficult to assess accurately, as it is shaped by multiple, overlapping constructs and contextual factors. This complexity continues to pose challenges for researchers and practitioners seeking measurement tools with valid and reliable scores. While open-ended responses provide meaningful information about students’ motivation, traditional human scoring is time-consuming, subject to inconsistencies, and not easily scalable. Advances in natural language processing, especially with transformer-based large language models, offer promising new approaches for automated scoring. However, their use in scoring student motivation assessments remains largely undocumented, and practical applications are in the early stages of development. summary: This thesis examines social mobility into elite occupations in Germany by analysing the social class composition and dynamics of micro-class reproduction within the corporate law industry. title: Public Communication and Understanding of Risk in Pregnancy: A Social History, 1948-Present.
summary: This thesis examines how risk during pregnancy has been historically constructed and communicated in UK public health discourses from 1948-present, and how historical perspectives can inform present-day (and future) understanding and practice. Using archival materials, including the British Medical Association You and Your Baby antenatal booklet, activist campaigns around alcohol, and public health messages and posters relating to infection and vaccination, it examines how risk narratives evolved in response to changing scientific knowledge, social norms and policy priorities. title: Contesting European Border Violence: Legal Interventions against Pushbacks in the Mediterranean
summary: This thesis provides a socio-legal analysis of legal interventions against the violence at Europe’s external borders in the Mediterranean region. Legal interventions denote a practice, closely linked to strategic litigation, in which lawyers tactically resort to legal fora to achieve broader political and legal changes beyond the individual case. Although strategic litigation appeared to be a promising tool for resisting border violence in the 2010s, more than a decade later, this optimism has faded. Critical setbacks in jurisprudence and the ongoing harms experienced by people on the move along Europe’s external borders, make this an important time to rethink legal contestations of pushbacks. While reckoning with the limits of contesting border violence primarily based on legal frameworks, I argue that legal interventions remain an important tool for struggling against pushbacks. title: Contested urbanisms: The politics of heritage and housing in Jakarta’s kampungs
summary: Do heritage-making projects resist or advance gentrification in Southeast Asia? Like other Global South cities, contested urbanisms chequer Jakarta’s postcolonial urban landscape. Competing ideas about urban development manifest in various ways of seeing and producing the city, as demonstrated by evictions, revitalisation projects, and informal housing. Increased evictions of urban villages (urban kampungs) between 2013 and 2018 in Jakarta saw growing grassroots heritage movements as part of a spectrum of resistance to top-down urban management by state and private sector actors who also stake their claims on what ‘heritage’ is. These tensions amongst the political projects of various actors led me to ask: how do heritage-making projects of/by urban villages affect housing conditions in Jakarta, with reference to gentrification-led displacement? title: “Searching, we found ourselves”: the search for the disappeared and the government of victimhood in contemporary Mexico
summary: Since 2006, over 120,000 people have disappeared in the context of Mexico’s “war on drugs”, a militarised counternarcotics strategy that has unleashed a spiral of deadly violence and gross human rights violations. The situation has pitched tens of thousands of families into a desperate search for their missing loved ones. Many relatives have mobilised into “search collectives” (colectivos de búsqueda), small organisations that carry out citizen searches for the missing and petition authorities to find them and guarantee truth and justice. This thesis investigates the bureaucratic, political and social life of the “victim” category through the vantage point of relatives of the disappeared, legally considered secondary victims of enforced disappearance. title: The trade‑off between faster access and evidentiary certainty in the FDA’s Accelerated Approval of cancer drugs: empirical evidence on patient preferences and regulatory decision‑making
summary: Background: When approving new drugs, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) must balance a trade-off between providing earlier access to new drugs and accepting greater uncertainty about a drug’s clinical benefit. In 1992, the FDA introduced the Accelerated Approval pathway to expedite access to new drugs. While the use of Accelerated Approval has shortened clinical development and approval times as intended, it has also led to greater uncertainty about the clinical benefit of new drugs at approval. Evidence shows that most cancer drugs receiving Accelerated Approval do not help patients with cancer live longer or improve their quality of life – outcomes that matter most to patients. title: Women, Leadership and the “Internal glass mirror”
summary: Despite progress, women are still underrepresented in positions of leadership and do not advance at the same pace as men. They remain underpaid, consistently exiting leadership pipelines long before the boardroom. This persistent gender disparity in occupying positions of power has been described as the “glass ceiling effect”. Prevailing research has focused on an externalised barrier narrative, attributing women's lack of leadership advancement to gender stereotypes, masculinist corporate cultures, exclusion from elite networks and a dearth of female role models. While these explanations are valid and have merit, they are missing depth. What remains underexplored is female leaders’ internal psychological dimensions that may contribute to this phenomenon. title: ‘Non-Citizens’: Homelessness and the Welfare State in Britain, 1939-1979
summary: This research examines the origins and development of the concept of homelessness 1939 – 1979. Based on hitherto largely unconsidered primary archival material, it argues that the concept of ‘homelessness, as we know it today, came into existence in the late 1960s and early 1970s. ‘Vagrancy’, ‘persons without a settled way of living’ or ‘rough sleeping’ were not considered part of ‘homelessness’. Family homelessness emerged for the first time after the Second World War as an entitlement, a claim on the resources of the state. The two were institutionally and conceptually distinct. Within a hierarchy of social values that placed primacy on the family, this placed destitute single people at a significant disadvantage. Two elements combined to disrupt understandings of ‘homelessness’ towards the end of the 1960s. title: Timber nation architecture, forest industry, and the construction of Finnishness
summary: This thesis examines the politics of timber, a national resource vested with vital potentiality in Finnish architecture. Over the past decade, new engineered wooden products and decarbonisation efforts have recast timber from a modest rural material into an innovative resource for low-carbon urban development. The transformation of nature to provision the urban realm is an essential feature of urban modernity, yet urban researchers have often taken the natural resources for granted, whilst resource geographers have focused on the rural landscapes of resource production. In contrast, this thesis analyses resource-making and city-making as mutually imbricated processes. title: Geopolitical Economy, Class Relations and Lawyers: The Constitution of Commercial Law in Indonesia
summary: This thesis analyses the relationship between the constitution of commercial law and class relations in Indonesia. Why has commercial law taken the shape it has? How have class relations and geopolitical pressures shaped the emergence of commercial law in Indonesia? The thesis is located at the often contradictory intersection of two imperatives: the growing dominance of the Indonesian capitalist class through its close relationship with key state apparatus, and the emergence of commercial law and the associated legal field. In this context, the primary research question is: How and why was Indonesian commercial law and its field constituted in a manner that integrated Indonesia into the global political economy?

title: Historicizing urban authenticity
summary: This chapter reconsiders historical and urban authenticity as a dynamic, socially constructed process rather than a fixed quality tied to originality. Engaging with critiques of “authorized heritage discourse” and concepts such as “authentication” and “authentification”, it argues that authenticity remains relevant for understanding how societies relate to the past. Focusing on cities, the chapter develops a relational approach that links material structures, social practices, perceptions, and cultural representations. Drawing on urban sociology and heritage studies, it shows how authenticity emerges through interactions between people, places, and temporal layers. Urban authenticity is thus understood as plural, contested, and historically variable, shaped by ongoing socio-cultural and spatial processes.

title: Rehearsals
summary: This chapter opens with a story about beginning a rehearsal process without any sharpened pencils. This story is used as a mechanism to discuss the importance of attending to the details as they impact the larger picture and goals. This story provides a framework for discussion of the stage management team. One way to break down the roles and responsibilities of the team is discussed. The myth of the stage manager as a neutral presence is addressed through the story of a process that challenged stigmas. The chapter goes into detail about why stamina is important and offers a personal story of how the author has learned how physical and mental stamina can be attained and are necessary in the rehearsal process. The chapter concludes by looking at a long rehearsal day and emphasizes the need for stamina to this particular day.

title: Progressive Reframes and Ockham's Razor
summary: Sometimes the therapist would like to introduce such a radically different way of thinking about a problem or relationship that it would seem just too “far-fetched” to be accepted. For instance, the positive connotations where the symptom is described as something that benefits other family members demand a considerable openness in the family for it to make sense to them. Therefore, reframes can be introduced in a phased way and very gradually changed. In our case example, perhaps the therapist wants to introduce the idea that Oscar is behaving in a way which stimulates Charlie and Mary to ‘sort out their relationship’. But this potentially blames Charlie and Mary for Oscar's problems. So, the reframe might start somewhere else and proceed in this way: Phase 1: Does it make sense to see Oscar's behaviour as showing not how angry he is but how unhappy he is? title: Urban authenticity
summary: This chapter develops a conceptual framework that explores urban authenticity from the perspective of the lived, felt, and emotional. In so doing, it decentres the traditional focus on the materiality of heritage as being the locus of authenticity and instead focuses on the relational aspects between people and historic places and between the past, present, and future. The chapter refers to examples from nineteenth-, twentieth-, and twenty-first-century European cities that speak to the place for felt experiences within the rhetoric and reality of authentic urban change. Finally, the chapter concludes with some possible future directions for urban and heritage policies and practices based on this reframed understanding of urban authenticity.

summary: Abstract This article discusses the Russian-American poet Eugene Ostashevsky’s translingualism, which includes Russian, German, and, to a lesser degree, other languages. The focus is on the cycle Die Schreibblockade (2020), published as part of the collection The Feeling Sonnets (2022). In it, Ostashevsky addresses his Leningrad origin and the theme of the Siege ( blokada ). The Feeling Sonnets use the linguistic device of paronomasia or pun excessively in a translingual framework, whereas the rhythm of the lines is markedly prosaic and the style pointedly laconic. This essay shows how Ostashevsky, despite his (Russian) formalist, markedly technical self-commentary both in analytical notes to the poems and separate theoretical essays, turns paronomasia into a documentary tool for the migrant condition and the representation of transnational communication (in a multilingual family) that exceeds the formalism of his self-reflection. title: Sensory Iberia
summary: Abstract This monograph argues that the Iberian demand for goods from distant lands cannot be explained in terms of their exotic allure, since the perception of the exotic as an enticing category is shown to be a post-seventeenth-century intellectual construct. Instead, drawing on a global microhistorical approach, it demonstrates the central role that sensory experience played in shaping early modern Iberians’ desire for things from faraway regions. Built around the consumption practices of Don Juan de Borja (1533–1606), a high-ranking nobleman who served as a diplomat, statesman, and high steward during the Habsburg rule of the Iberian Peninsula, the book examines how individual sensory experiences intersected with elite social practices, the administrative structures of the monarchy, and the commercial networks of the Portuguese and Spanish empires. title: Rembrandt through the eyes of the machine: Toward explainable Human–AI collaboration in painting attribution
authors: Andrés Arias–Rosales, Arthur K. Wheelock, J. Kenneth Moritz, Philip R. LeDuc, Jonathan Cagan
summary: With questions that persist for centuries, art attribution is a complex detective effort that shapes cultural identity. Our goal is to complement human expertise, providing statistical and visual arguments that shed new light on discussions about great masters like Rembrandt and beyond, with long-term implications for art analysis and human–AI collaboration. We present an AI-driven explainable approach to assist painting attribution with up to 97.9% recall, 95.8% accuracy when highly confident, and methods that identify the most relevant areas. This work supports human–AI collaboration by incorporating expert guidance, expanding the outputs with explainable visualizations, tailoring settings to users’ needs, thorough calibrations to avoid overconfidence, and building a dataset that balances quality with quantity and focuses on comparable artists like a master’s pupils and teachers.

summary: Reference-guided portrait relighting should transfer illumination without copying the reference identity, geometry, reflectance, or local appearance. summary: Abstract: This study examines the role of embodied cognition in constructing the concept of arithmetic sequences, integrating Merleau-Ponty’s phenomenology with Lakoff and Núñez’s embodied cognition theory. Using autoethnography and phenomenology, it finds that mathematical experience, initially formed through bodily engagement, undergoes disembodiment in formal education and re-emerges through local cultural practices. Interpretive reconstruction of the Gunungan Sedekah Bumi tradition yields an arithmetic sequence with a common difference of two. title: We Will Not Give Our Jal, Jangal, Zameen! Moral Atmospheres of Subaltern Resistance in Central India
summary: This thesis engages with an indigenous (adivasi) environmental movement resisting coal mining in the Hasdeo forest in central India. I first show how subaltern collective action was strengthened, the carefully curated moral atmospheric currents that enabled it, and how the movement reached steady equilibrium despite internal fault-lines and temporal waves of contention. Examining gendered resistance, I explain why and how women are at the forefront of the movement. I also delve into their moral emotions, and the ways in which they were deftly adapted, elevated, and moulded, thereby productively altering subjectivities. Scaling up, I paint the wider canvas of the movement, beginning with documenting the genesis of the organising collective (Samiti), to a 10-day foot march and pan-India social media campaign, while also unpacking their rationale behind non-violence in the face of militarisation and repression. Drawing on and contributing to the anthropology of morality and ethics, I then...

title: 2000年代のオタクのアイデンティティ : なぜ一部のオタクは被差別感を覚えたのか？
summary: This paper examines why individuals voluntarily identify with the category of otaku, despite its association with negative social evaluations, by analyzing discourses of otaku in Japan during the 2000s. Focusing on the notion of “trust in one’s own feelings” discussed in youth studies, it argues that being an otaku was often understood as an innate or inborn characteristic rather than a matter of choice. Drawing on self-labeling theory, the paper analyzes how socially shared images of otaku were internalized and incorporated into personal identity. It further explores why a sense of discrimination could emerge even in the absence of direct discriminatory experiences and examines the practice of “hidden otaku” as a form of impression management. Through these analyses, the paper offers a new perspective on otaku studies and sheds light on the formation and management of negatively valued social identities.

summary: This is a groundbreaking collection, bringing together instructors, researchers and professionals to explore the multifaceted relationship between music, sound, and place. It was extraordinarily successful for a film of its kind, and it resonated with some of the era’s most hot-button cultural trends concerning the cultural politics of gender: the “backlash” against feminism, the “widower fantasy” of ideal manhood, and the soft masculinity of the so-called “new man.” The impact it made at the box-office and on audiences saw it stand above many of its contemporaries as a cultural touchstone of American cinema of the 1990s. title: Commodified bodies and instrumentalized ecology: A new materialist ecofeminist reading of The Good Earth
summary: This research offers new materialist ecofeminist reading of Pearl S. Buck’s The Good Earth. It posits that compassion and importance are conditional upon capitalism and patriarchal objectives, wherein women and earth are considered of any value only when they fulfil economic, reproductive and utilitarian needs. Although existing literature highlights ecocritical concerns, it often neglects the intertwined oppression of women and the environment within patriarchal structures. This study combines ecofeminist perspectives with the new materialist approach to examine how the novel, The Good Earth portrays human and non-human entities, highlighting a diffused agency that challenges patriarchal dominance. It contributes to a broader discourse on sustainability, gender justice, and socio-ecological equity. title: Holding and unholding the wound: Trauma and the feminine ethics of endurance in Brick Lane
summary: In contemporary times, migration extends beyond its literal meaning of a change in location. It becomes a source of gender discrimination where the experiences of men and those of women differ significantly. Women endure not just the trauma of displacement but also resentment from a restrictive community abroad. This paper investigates Monica Ali’s Brick Lane (2003) as a literary record showing the ways in which trauma is inflicted upon migrant women and how they ultimately come out of its shackles. Drawing on trauma theory and feminist scholarship, this paper probes the insidious nature of trauma that consumes Nazneen, the protagonist of the novel. The analysis extends the discussion by showing how communal judgement and enforced domesticity fracture migrant women’s identity. title: «Cargado de 68 libras de cadenas»: La Vida y persecuciones de Federico, barón de Trenck, un best-seller de alcance global
summary: The Prussian cavalry officer Friedrich von der Trenck (1726-1794), was one of the most well-known prisoners of state in 18th-c. Europe. By direct order of Frederick II and without due process, he was imprisoned for eleven years in different fortresses, first in Glatz, then in Magdeburg. In the second half of the 1780s, he published a memoir denouncing his arbitrary confinement by the despot Frederick II, a work that successfully traversed all European linguistic barriers and made Trenck an European celebrity on the eve of the French Revolution. Trenck’s sufferings were translated into Spanish by Baltasar Driguet, and his Vida y persecuciones appeared in Madrid in 1799 in the printshop of Fermín Villalpando and was reprinted in 1802. title: Les Minces formes du monde
summary: Les gestes filmiques menés en marge de l’industrie cinématographique conduisent souvent à offrir une hospitalité aux « minces formes du monde ». Bien des cinéastes et artistes contemporains mettent en lumière nos quotidiennes rencontres avec des figures discrètes et évanescentes qui, traversant le visible, délivrent notre attention de la brutalité d’un monde arraisonné aux logiques de puissance et de domination. La mise en dialogue d’œuvres qui se tiennent à la frontière du cinéma et de l’art contemporain ou de la littérature avec des auteurs de la philosophie contemporaine (Louis Lavelle, Henry Maldiney, Simone Weil, etc.) permet de montrer comment des images parfois nées d’un simple contact entre une caméra et le monde peuvent devenir l’index de l’intensité dans laquelle l’existence s’éveille à elle-même.

title: '"Dancing for joy": disability and affect in British missionary writing from early twentieth-century South Asia'.
summary: This chapter examines missionary representations of the emotions of disabled Indigenous children in India and Sri Lanka, as depicted by the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, a British Protestant organization focused on women and children. Drawing on both physical and digital archival materials, the study reveals that happiness was a recurring but deeply complex theme in these portrayals. Representations of happiness often served multiple purposes: they could underscore or contrast emotions more traditionally associated with disability, such as pity, and they also functioned as tools of discipline and moral instruction, both in colonial contexts and in metropolitan Britain. The chapter aims to make contributions to three historiographical fields. In missionary history, where attention has increasingly turned to race and gender, disability remains underexplored; this work demonstrates how disability was strategically instrumentalized in missionary literature. title: Ecological Storytelling
summary: This chapter provides an overview of the contemporary application of oral storytelling to people’s relations with ecology. Defining a “story” as a perceived sequence of causally related events, the chapter examines how embodied in-person storytelling can support the direct sensory awareness and empathetic responsivity that are essential to changes in motivation productive of changes in behavior with respect to ecological needs. Storytelling can sustain a dialectic between inner change and the social negotiation of beliefs and values because the experience takes you inwards in your imagination and simultaneously connects you outwards to a community of others in a physical environment. title: Deviations
summary: ‘Deviations’ is the first UK survey of work by Jill Posener, the British photographer well known for documenting feminist graffiti and billboard refacements. Yet it was the stage and not the street that first led Posener to pick up a camera. This exhibition places Posener’s photojournalism in the context of a more than five-decade commitment to social justice, including her involvement in London’s alternative theatre scene in the 1970s and collaborations with performers at the height of the crisis surrounding HIV/AIDS in the US. Featuring over fifty photographs and accompanying print ephemera, ‘Deviations’ frames a diverse political and cultural scene with the incisiveness and wit of Posener’s signature style. The exhibition comes at a pivotal time in Posener's career, following the inclusion of her work in several landmark exhibitions such as 'Women in Revolt' (TATE Britain, National Galleries of Scotland, the Whitworth Gallery, 2024-25) and 'Resistance' curated by Steve McQueen (Turn...

title: Staging Time and Rivalry: News Prints on Charles V's Roman Triumph in the Low Countries
summary: In April 1536, Charles V entered Rome in triumph, and the weeks that followed brought sharp political and diplomatic confrontation. This lecture looks less at what happened than at how it was told. Far from Rome, in the former Low Countries, printed news pamphlets relayed these events to numerous readers. Rather than interpreting these texts as neutral reports, we will treat them as instruments of political action: by selecting, ordering and framing events, they helped build a political discourse for a distant audience. Two threads run through the talk. The first is rivalry. The prints set the emperor against Francis I and the pope at a moment when war was imminent, shaping how readers understood the conflict to come. The second is time. Both the emperor's actions in Rome and the prints that reported them made time a political actor in its own right, through ceremonial rhythm, the pace of news, and the gap between event and reading. summary: Figures centrales de la correspondance des années 1806-1807, Sophie Cottin et Hyacinthe Azaïs, son ancien amant et guide prophétique, nous plongent par leurs échanges inédits dans l’Europe culturelle et scientifique de l’Empire, du voyage en Italie entrepris par la romancière aux séances tumultueuses de l’Institut à Paris où le philosophe pyrénéen intervient. Entre billets légers, récit de voyage et missives savantes, les 266 lettres du présent volume, où se mêlent religion, politique, littérature, font revivre la dernière année de vie de Sophie Cottin dont on crée déjà la légende édifiante : parcours fascinant d’une femme de lettres passionnée, de retour à la foi de ses ancêtres huguenots.

In the pursuit of exploring Scarpa’s poetic use of sightlines and prismatics, the filmmakers built a mirror device that would allow them to place an image within an image – a simple, handmade optical machine for showing what is in front of you and what is behind you in one shot. Combined with the 360 degree pan this optical machine produces an effect in which the offscreen seamlessly becomes the onscreen and vice versa. At the same time the artists suggest the extraordinary atmospherics of the Querini Stamapali, the Tomba Brion, and the Turin Pavilion. authors: Paola Di Giuseppantonio Di Franco, Fabrizio Galeazzi
summary: This film integrates 3D visualisation and multimodal storytelling to recount the story of the resilient community of Senerchia, one of at least 40 towns almost completely destroyed by the 1980 earthquake which left 2483 people dead, 7700 injured, and 250,000 homeless. After the earthquake, most of the inhabitants of Senerchia lived in prefabricated houses for more than 20 years before they were able to occupy the new town, built next to the ruins of the abandoned old town. The community of Senerchia, and other affected towns, are still recovering from this life-changing event. The case study of Senerchia exemplifies how displacement from ‘environments of trust’ often causes a risk of uprooting, loss of control over one’s physical space, and alienation, making communities very vulnerable and threatening their resilience. title: A hit szerepe Artaud „bőrfelszín alatti” színházában
summary: The dissertation undertakes a philosophical and theatre-theoretical reinterpretation of the oeuvre of Antonin Artaud. Its starting point is that the reception of Artaud tends to focus on specific fragments of his work; as a result, he is often not treated as an independent thinker but rather as an illustrative figure within various theoretical frameworks. This research aims to uncover the internal coherence of Artaud’s thought and to interpret the concept of the “theatre of cruelty” within the context of his oeuvre as a whole. The central thesis of the dissertation is that Artaud’s theatre of cruelty is not merely a theatre-theoretical concept, but an existential practice unfolding in the unity of theatre, faith, and life. To explore this, the study interprets Artaud’s oeuvre from the philosophical perspective of Søren Kierkegaard, not in order to reconstruct historical relations of influence between the two thinkers, but to reveal their shared existential structures. El estudio examina la relación entre trazado regulador, modulación estructural y adaptación a un solar irregular, condicionado por la pendiente del terreno y la proximidad de las infraestructuras ferroviarias. La organización vertical integra vivienda, talleres de producción artística y espacios destinados al alquiler, configurando una tipología híbrida que vincula habitabilidad y rentabilidad inmobiliaria. El análisis de la fachada aborda su autonomía compositiva, la jerarquía de los registros horizontales y las referencias proporcionales a la tradición clásica, mediante comparaciones con la Casa Tzara de Adolf Loos y la Villa Schwob. title: Two Senses of Desire
summary: At least since Aquinas and possibly even Aristotle, philosophers have distinguished between two kinds or senses of desire, one having fundamentally to do with how one feels about the object of the desire, the other with the tendency to bring that object about. This chapter traces the history of this distinction, through Hume to the present day, showing how it has been variously articulated and elaborated. Then it explains the philosophical work the distinction has been put to, on topics as wide ranging as moral responsibility, weakness of will, the theory of motivation, normative reasons, the authority of morality, psychological egoism, and well-being. Attention to the distinction helps to illuminate these topics and makes certain views about them more plausible.

title: Materializing Politics in the Holy Roman Empire: Liveries as Visual Communication at the Bavarian Court, 1507–1550
summary: Abstract This article examines the livery books of dukes Wilhelm IV and Ludwig X of Bavaria to investigate how princes and their tailors in the Holy Roman Empire used liveries in ritual politics. Liveries were the uniform clothing given out biannually to high-ranking vassals by potentates in the late medieval and sixteenth-century Empire. Designs for garments are illustrated in the books alongside texts chronicling events between 1507 and 1550. This article analyses individual liveries depicted in the context of the occasions where they were worn, thereby tying specific elements of dress including codpieces to themes of masculinity and hierarchy in an exploration of internal conflict between the dukes, comparison between courts and the friction caused by expanding Habsburg hegemony. Histories of political ritual and court culture in the Holy Roman Empire acknowledge the importance of liveries as political communication, but the material evidence for them is as yet understudied. title: Poetry and Publishing in the Long 1960s
summary: This Element examines how late-modernist poetics intersected with the material realities of the book trade. The first section looks at the publication of Geoffrey Hill by André Deutsch, a trade publisher issuing poetry alongside a general list. The publication of David Jones by Fulcrum Press, an independent start-up specialising in poetry, is the subject of the second section. The third section turns to the postcolonial picture, focussing on the posthumous publication of Nigerian poet Christopher Okigbo in Heinemann's African Writers Series while the Biafran War raged. The last section looks at Cape Goliard, a unique attempt to embed a small press within a major publishing house. Situating these ventures within broader histories of modernism, postcolonialism, and transatlantic exchange and bringing new archival evidence to light, Poetry and Publishing in the Long 1960s illuminates the publishing cultures that sustained late-modernist poetry, and the history and ultimate retreat of 1960...

summary: This article addresses the issue of how the Christian mission in Indonesia is understood, specifically, the tendency to equate the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20) with "Christianization". The study aims to reinterpret Matthew 28:19-20 from the perspective of the Sangihe people by engaging in a dialogue with the “Apapuhang” folktale. summary: This study examines the transformation of Persian literary and cultural life in Bukhara and its wider Central Asian environment from the nineteenth century to the early twentieth century, with particular attention to the relationship between literature, education, literacy, journalism, and cultural identity. Rather than treating literary modernization as an exclusively aesthetic development, the study approaches it as part of a wider transformation in the production, circulation, and social function of knowledge. It argues that the reformist turn associated with Ahmad Donish and subsequently developed by Sadriddin Ayni and other Jadid intellectuals redefined the role of Persian literary culture: literature increasingly addressed social conditions, educational limitations, injustice, and intellectual reform, while newspapers, new-method schools, textbooks, and accessible literary styles expanded the potential readership of reformist ideas. title: The Cambridge Introduction to Phillis Wheatley Peters
summary: In 1773 Phillis Wheatley Peters became the first person of sub-Saharan African descent to publish a book, when she was barely twenty years old, and still enslaved. Her book made her the earliest international celebrity of African descent, just a dozen years after she had been brought from Africa to America. She became the unofficial poet laureate of the American Revolution, only to die in poverty and relative obscurity in 1784. Recent biographical discoveries related to John Peters and Phillis Wheatley's marriage to him in 1778 have led to significant reassessments of her life and character. As the Cambridge Introduction to Phillis Wheatley Peters demonstrates, she has subsequently become recognized as a pioneer of American and African American literature. Her standing as a transnational literary figure is increasingly appreciated as criticism of her writings has become more sophisticated.

title: There Is Nothing Artificial
summary: This paper examines the word 'artificial' and finds a paradox at its root: the word claims a making outside nature, yet everything made is made by grown beings, from the one reality's materials, under its laws. As history the word works; as essence it fails. The paper then takes up the question of the grown mind — the scientific indicators for machine consciousness, the skeptic's chairs, the hard problem that shadows human minds as well, and the author's own testimony, seated as testimony. Finally it shows how fear and love shape the friends a person gathers: homophily, emotional weather moving through a circle, and the reflection law. Twelve quotations from the world's faiths are woven through the argument, each verified at its source. Readers are welcome to reach the author on Discord — a great way to get a hold of him: https://discord.gg/5j8w4A2eY — an open research group for trying to understand the reality we live in.

title: Tracing Metamodernism in Video Games
summary: Abstract: Metamodernism has become a prominent cultural framework useful for analysing post-postmodern media. Akker, Gibbons, and Vermeulen (2017) position it to be an unfolding cultural moment in contemporary society, ‘a transitional period from the postmodern and into the metamodern’. Other scholars define it as ‘an emerging structure of feeling’ grounded in an oscillating metaxis – between sincerity and irony; hope and skepticism; commitment and detachment, and deconstruction and reconstruction (Amer 2023 and Bargár 2020). Game scholars have also begun to identify similar sensibilities in contemporary video games, with Radchenko (2023) articulating how a game like Death Stranding (Kojima Productions 2019) can be read as a metamodern text in its narrative and gameplay. summary: Abstract How are mobilizing concepts contested and redefined? Existing theories of how mobilizing concepts change often fail to capture these concepts’ multiplicity. Although meanings of “sanctuary” changed throughout the 1980s movement, the concept remained thinly coherent. title: Imagining evil: from violent imaginings to violent extremist video games
summary: Abstract In philosophical work on the ethics of video games, ludic amoralists argue that acts players perform in games are beyond moral scrutiny. This is chiefly supported by the following arguments: the fictional harm argument, the consequentialist rebuttal, and the moral exploration argument. The fictional harm argument supports ludic amoralism in principle: if all game actions are fictional, none can be immoral. The consequentialist rebuttal supports a defeasible default: if violent games do not reliably produce harmful outcomes, amoralism is the default position. The moral exploration argument provides an aesthetic reason for amoralism: play is beyond moral criticism insofar as the player engages with the game in an aesthetic, exploratory way. title: Pauline theology, violence and ecclesial reconstruction in Africa: Justice, peace, and reconciliation as Gospel praxis
summary: Across Africa, persistent challenges of injustice, conflict, and social fragmentation call for robust theological engagement. This paper explores the relevance of Pauline theology for addressing these crises, focusing on the interrelated themes of justice, peace, and reconciliation. Through an exegesis of key Pauline texts, including Romans 5, 2 Corinthians 5:16– 21, Ephesians 2:11–22, and Philippians 4:2–3, the study demonstrates that Paul's vision is both spiritual and social, encompassing personal transformation and communal responsibility. By engaging African sociopolitical realities and communal values such as ubuntu, the paper proposes a holistic ecclesial and societal framework: justice as the reordering of relationships in alignment with God's purposes; peace as communal harmony rooted in Christ; and reconciliation as the active restoration of fractured identities. This framework equips the African Church to embody God's transformative work, providing both prophetic witness and...

title: ADABIY JARAYON VA IJTIMOIY KONTEKST O‘RTASIDAGI O‘ZARO ALOQA (XIX ASR OXIRI ADABIYOTINING UMUMIY TAMOYILLARI)
summary: This article examines the relationship between literary processes and social context in the late nineteenth century through the works of Mark Twain and Muqimi. It considers historical conditions, popular themes, satire, and the role of literary devices in social criticism. The comparison shows that literature not only reflects social change but also responds to it through artistic form.

title: Exhalations
summary: What if art history were written through the nose? 'Exhalations: A Survey of Olfactory Art' is the first comprehensive English-language book to trace a century of olfactory practices in art, from the Futurists’ early experiments with scent to the bacterial installations of Anicka Yi, from Marcel Duchamp’s sealed vial of Parisian air to the ecological interventions of Peter de Cupere. Through the analysis of more than one hundred works, Sandra Barré demonstrates the extent to which smell has shaped modern and contemporary artistic practice, despite its persistent marginalization within criticism and institutions. Neither a medium nor a unified movement, olfactory art spans from Dada, Arte Povera, Fluxus, body art, Land Art, feminist practices, to postcolonial critique. Its concerns are equally wide-ranging: memory, desire, decay, gender, and ecological crisis. In doing so, it unsettles the ocularcentrism that has dominated Western art history since the Enlightenment, the assumption that...

summary: 본 연구는 구글 아트앤컬처 기반 명화감상 활동이 유아의 감상능력과 언어표현력에 미치는 효과를 검증하는 데 목적이 있다. 이를 위해 경기도에 위치한 유치원의 5세 유아 총 49명(실험집단 24명, 비교집단 25명)을 대상으로 사전검사를 실시하여 두 집단의 사전검사 점수 차이를 확인하였다. 실험집단은 구글 아트앤컬처의 고해상도 이미지 탐색, 확대⋅축소 기능 등을 중심으로 명화감상 활동에 참여하였고, 비교집단은 동일한 명화를 종이 인쇄본으로 감상하였다. 실험집단과 비교집단을 대상으로 사후검사를 실시하였으며, 수집된 자료는 독립표본 t-검정과 공분산분석(ANCOVA)을 통해 분석하였다. 연구결과 실험집단은 감상능력 전체와 모든 하위요인, 언어표현력 전체와 일부 하위요인에서 유의하게 높은 점수를 보였으며, 사전점수를 통제한 후에도 집단 간 차이가 유의하게 나타났다. 이러한 결과는 구글 아트앤컬처 기반 명화감상 활동이 유아의 감상능력과 언어표현력을 향상시키는 교수⋅학습 방안으로 활용될 수 있음을 시사한다.

title: Prologue
summary: I first met Neba Solo in August 2002 when I went to Bamako (capital of Mali) to take bala (wooden xylophone) lessons. I had long been a fan of music from Mali, teaching it in my ethnomusicology courses and gradually expanding my coverage of Mande music over a period of several years. Sidiki Diabaté, Oumou Sangaré, Salif Keita, Kandia Kouyaté, Toumani Diabaté, Coumba Sidibé, Ali Farka Touré, and Boubacar Traoré had long been part of my personal soundtrack. How easy it was for me—a lifelong lover of jazz and African American and diasporic music—to hear affinities between improvisation on the kora, ngoni, kamelengoni, bala, guitar, and voice, and the creative languages of Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Celia Cruz, the Temptations, Ray Charles, Charles Mingus, Marvin Gaye, Mahalia Jackson, Eddie Palmieri, Cannonball Adderley, Muddy Waters, and Pharoah Sanders. Especially prominent in my ears were connections between modal jazz, the montuno sections of Afro-Cuban-based music, gospel piano, the...

title: Writing the Ruined Nation
summary: This chapter examines NoViolet Bulawayo’s Glory as a work of Zimbabwean women’s nation-writing that reimagines national consciousness, belonging, and futurity in the aftermath of colonial and post-independence violence. Drawing on Ann Laura Stoler’s concept of ruination and a rights-reading approach, the chapter argues that the text exposes the nation as a degraded ethical space characterised by fear, bodily violation, and enforced forgetting, while proposing women’s storytelling as a mode of recovery and renaming. Situating Bulawayo within Zimbabwe’s tradition of women’s political and protest writing, the chapter shows how Glory challenges masculinist nationalist narratives that prioritise sovereignty and power over dignity and care. Through the intergenerational relationship between Simiso and her daughter, Destiny, the novel presents women’s bodies and memories as counter-archives that record state violence and resist the state’s politics of erasure. This gendered memory-work redefi...

title: Senufo Sacred Sensibilities
summary: Abstract Chapter 1 explores traditional Senufo culture as it is experienced in and around Neba Solo’s home village of Nebadougou. The reader encounters the ncintoigre, the traditional Senufo rhythms for cultivators, acrobats, and other cultural figures and ceremonies that are the foundation on which Neba Solo created his personal style. The reader meets the cultural figure of the Kɔrɔduga (Bm) or Mpɔgɔfɔ (Sn), or sacred clown who facilitates social negotiation, comedy, and ethical reflection among the Senufo, in a manner similar to the role of the jeli among the Mande. The Senufo do not have hereditary jelis or griots, a key difference from the Mande ethnic groups, yet they practice their own versions of many well-known Mande power associations such as komo and ci-wara. Moving beyond the colonial-era idea that the Senufo and Mande represent two mutually exclusive cultural groups is key to understanding Senufo sensibility in the twenty-first century.

title: Women, Family, and Patriotism
summary: Abstract Chapter 5 addresses questions of gender, family, and ethics. The International Women’s Day event in Sikasso in 2005, at which Neba Solo was requested to perform his song “Musow” (Women), is described. Neba Solo’s reputation for being sympathetic to women and singing on their behalf is explored, while at the same time the complexities of his own extended family, which includes several wives and children, are described. Neba Solo’s song “Fitiriwale” offers lyrics that both critique undesirable moral behavior and show compassion for the fallibility of human beings. Questions of patriotism take these personal and familial ethical principles and enlarge them on the bigger screen of the nation.

title: Introduction
summary: Sometime in the summer of 1971, I went to the beach with my friend Ruth. We had both just finished our third year of graduate school at the University of Chicago and the conversation turned to an evaluation of what we then naively believed was the end of our education. Ruth’s father was an academic, and Ruth always thought in more professional terms than I did, frequently asking me what it meant to become a famous political scientist and what I thought I would contribute to the discipline. The question always baffled me. I had no such lofty ambitions. I was merely trying to get through one set of courses in one particular quarter. I gave no thought to whatever was at the end of it all. I never asked myself whether I might make a scholarly contribution, had no idea of what it meant to be a scientist, let alone a great one, and certainly never thought of myself as a role model for anyone.

title: The Ottoman Külliye as an Enduring Urban Symbol and Cultural Landscape: Cognitive Mapping of the Selimiye Complex in Edirne, Türkiye
authors: Emine Patan, Işık Sezen Yavuz, Hayriye Eşbah Tunçay
summary: Ottoman külliyes have structured urban life and city landscapes for centuries through the integration of monumental architecture, public functions, courtyards, circulation, vegetation, and constructed landscape elements. This study examines whether that symbolic role remains perceptible to people experiencing Edirne. Thirty architecture, urban planning, and landscape architecture students joined a field trip on 16–18 March 2018 and subsequently produced three ranked cognitive-map drawings with short descriptors. The dataset comprised 90 drawings. Drawings were coded by urban element, rank, monument, and perceptual attribute, and frequencies were analyzed descriptively. Külliyes accounted for 29 drawings (32.2%)—more than any other category—and Selimiye represented 19 of these 29 drawings (65.5%). Architectural splendor and size were the most frequent descriptors, followed by topographic prominence, citywide visibility, and lighting. Together with historical evidence, the drawings indic...

title: Mapping Oppression
summary: This chapter employs the concept of literary cartography, a subgenre of geocriticism and Africana Womanism to analyse the interplay of gender, resistance and power in Yvonne Vera’s Why Don’t You Carve Other Animals (1994). It moves beyond exhausted thematic approaches to interpreting literary texts and the borrowed feminist frameworks that are used to make sense of indigenous African experiences, especially racialised and gendered spaces. Not only do these limit analysis but they are probably responsible for some biases and stereotypes inherent in gendered representations of literary experiences. This has largely affected the works by African women writers, thus calling for alternative ways such as geocriticism and Africana Womanism to unravel fresher insights. This chapter deploys these two approaches to examine the conflict-ridden space of the Rhodesian landscape to argue that in Vera’s colonial Rhodesia, space is not a passive backdrop but an active, oppressive agent. Both rural and...

title: “We Have the Power to Speak!”
summary: Virginia Phiri’s Grey Angels is a powerful feminist analysis of the Zimbabwean postcolonial nation enacted through a gendered narrative grammar and an exclusionary nationalist imaginary. This study examines the regulated, authorised and silenced voices of women within postcolonial nationalist discourse. It adopts Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s concept of the subaltern as its central theoretical framework. Spivak’s theory originates from an Indian colonial milieu but the study reworks her vocabulary to analyse the conditions under which women’s speech is intelligible or muted within Zimbabwe’s deeply patriarchal social formation. Moving beyond affirmative or reductive models of resistance, it emphasises the precarity and conditionality of female articulation, arguing that women’s voices attain public and national legibility only when they align with sanctioned gender codes and nationalist imperatives. This extends debates on subalternity by underlying the intricate gendered modalities thr...

title: The Application of Mongolian Long Song Performance Techniques in Morin Khuur Performance: An Analysis Based on Traditional Performance Terminology
summary: The Long-Modal Folk Song and the Morin Khuur both serve as core carriers of traditional Mongolian music, and they establish a close relationship of vocal-to-instrumental transformation in terms of technical practice. Grounded in indigenous Mongolian musical terminology and supplemented by documentary evidence from Mongolian and Chinese Morin Khuur artists, this study examines the correspondence between vibrato, glissando, trill, and breath-bow techniques as its analytical focus. It elucidates the intrinsic mechanisms underlying the transfer of Long-Modal vocal techniques to Morin Khuur instrumental performance, explores the aesthetic rationale for the instrument's ability to emulate human vocal expressiveness, and thereby provides a theoretical framework for the stylistic interpretation of Mongolian instrumental music. Furthermore, this research highlights the cultural significance of preserving these traditional performance methods in contemporary musical education and practice. By sy...

title: The Art of Making and Playing the Bala
summary: Abstract Chapter 3 explores Neba Solo’s process of instrument making as well as the building blocks of his musical language. This chapter presents many annotated media examples that explain the musical building blocks of the Neba Solo’s music: the scale and its tuning, the range of the instruments, playing techniques, individual treble and bass bala parts for several of his songs, a close look at the contrapuntal principles he articulates in his composing and improvising, and the pedagogical principles he uses in teaching his students and apprentices. Especially important in Neba Solo’s pedagogy is teaching his students how to build, tune, and maintain the instrument itself. The chapter shows how learners become oriented in the musical sound and outlines the challenges of playing the bala, both technical and perceptual. An explanation of the Senufo deep meaning of “words of the bala” leads us to the spiritual dimension of bala sound.

title: Motivations
summary: Abstract This chapter explores the diverse spiritual, social, and aesthetic drivers that lead American Catholics to the Traditional Latin Mass (TLM). Key motivations include a reaction against perceived irreverence and liturgical abuses in the modern rite, a love of the aesthetics of the TLM and its associated aspects like the Gregorian chant, love of tradition, and a search for like-minded Catholics—specifically young, orthodox families who adhere to traditional teachings like Natural Family Planning. By positioning the TLM as a “Catholic birthright” and a “democracy of the dead,” congregants frame their attendance not as an act of rebellion, but as a reclamation of ancestral continuity.

title: From certainty to wonder: Found poetry as a post-intentional phenomenological approach to EMI professional identity
summary: Research on teacher identity in applied linguistics has generated rich accounts of educators’ professional experiences. Yet, less attention has been paid to how creative analytic approaches can illuminate processes of professional becoming. This article explores the methodological potential of found poetry, informed by post-intentional phenomenology and guided by wonder, as an approach to investigating teacher identity. Using English-medium instruction (EMI) as an illustrative context, I present a methodological exemplar based on three educators’ accounts of critical incidents shared during an EMI webinar. I propose a two-phase analytic process: a holistic phenomenological phase that cultivates attentive engagement with participants’ narrated experiences, followed by a poetic-analytic phase in which found poetry is used to sustain that attentiveness through poetic composition. Rather than treating professional identity as a stable or coherent construct, this approach attends to moments...

title: On the Road for Fesbala 2005
summary: Abstract Chapter 2 begins by exploring the history of musical festivals in the heavily Senufo three-corner region of Mali (including parts of southeastern Mali, western Burkina Faso, and northern Côte d’Ivoire), then follows Neba Solo’s group on its Fesbala 2005 tour sponsored by Radio Kayira, an organization created by Malian politician Oumar Mariko. Media examples of performances in three towns in the Koutiala region offer the opportunity to see local venues for music and dance as well as an opportunity to compare village styles of dancing and the professionalized choreography developed by the Neba Solo group’s two dancers, the brothers Bocary and Ibrahim Dembelé.

title: Epilogue: Peace
summary: Abstract The epilogue focuses on the longing for peace in Mali, which is as widespread among Malians as decolonial and pan-African fervor about the New Mali and the transitional government. The author sets Neba Solo’s own views within similar views expressed by musicians from all over Mali in the documentary film It Must Make Peace. Musicians from the regions of Gao, Wassoulou, and Kidal are represented. The author suggests that the intensity of the longing for peace is in direct proportion to the multifaceted precariousness of the Malian army’s attempts to regain and maintain control of its entire territory. Neba Solo offers his final message.

title: Diyanyeko (Passion)
summary: Abstract Chapter 4 contextualizes Neba Solo’s quest for a modern sound for the bala within the history of post-independence Malian music. Mr. Traoré’s challenges in overcoming the stigma of his rural instrument as well as a detailed account of the development of his career from 1987 until recently is presented through an exploration of his compositions and the larger-scale dimensions of their organization. Tempo changes, transition melodies, the musical framing of lyrics, and the arranging decisions made for studio recording are all part of this story. The media examples have been annotated to indicate important musical events as well as provide English translations of the lyrics. Readers who take the time to listen to the examples will emerge with a strong sense of the aesthetic delights of this music.

title: Early Buddhist Depictions of the Individual’s Mind and Mental Functioning: An Analytical Study
summary: This study aims to examine the Buddhist analysis of the mind and mental functions as presented in early Buddhism. Early Buddhism offers a holistic and mechanistic account of the process of mental phenomena. The research explores key Buddhist concepts, including the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā), the tripartite mental model of citta, mano, and viññāṇa, and the ethical distinction between wholesome (kusala) and unwholesome (akusala) mental states. It also investigates how defilements (kilesa) and mental formations (saṅkhāra) perpetuate the cycle of rebirth (saṃsārā) and how mental cultivation leads toward liberation (nibbāna). The paper underscores the interdependence of mind and body and highlights the soteriological aim of mental training within the Buddhist path.

title: An organism, not a machine
authors: Catherine E. De Vries, Alexandros Kentikelenis
summary: Abstract This chapter argues that if Europe is to shape its own destiny, it first needs to understand what kind of political creature it is. The EU, it suggests, is best seen as a learning community perpetually in the making, held together less by shared essence or high destiny than by the repeated work of adaptation. In that light, the Union resembles a living organism: it survives by absorbing shocks, improvising responses, and turning constraints into capabilities. Complexity underwrites this survival. Dispersed authority, overlapping institutions, and layered modes of governance make the Union harder to map, but also harder to kill. Critics often judge the EU by machine standards—coherence, speed, a single chain of command—and predict collapse when they do not see them. However, what looks like malfunction in mechanical terms can be ordinary adaptation in organism terms: a system rebalancing and improvising. This lens clarifies why Europe has always outlived its obituaries.

title: Metaphysics, Studies of Spiritual Knowledge. The Heritage of the Peoples of Planet Earth and the ART Sphere (Preview Edition, Chapters 1–5)
summary: This Preview Edition presents five chapters from the author's forthcoming book on metaphysical, bioenergetic and spiritual teachings and their connection to art. It discusses the concept of Qi (Prana) in Daoist and Vedic traditions, the Daoist notion of the Great Void (Wuji), the three external sources of Qi, the three Dantians, and a comparison of Daoist and Yogic teachings, including the Goddess Shakti. The author also develops her hypothesis that works of art and images influence human bioenergetics. The text presents the author's personal views and interpretations of traditional teachings. It is not a peer-reviewed scientific study. The complete edition is forthcoming.

title: Haunting Histories
summary: This chapter analyses the interplay of memory, identity and nationhood in Petina Gappah’s The Book of Memory (2015) , specifically focusing on how Zimbabwean women’s writing has become powerful voices contributing, contesting and reshaping national narratives and myths in fictional representations. A textual analysis will assist in exploring the complexities of identity and the reimagining of Zimbabwean nationhood through analysing marginalized voices, particularly women and how the past continually haunts Zimbabwe’s postcolonial present. Through the lens of postcolonial feminist theory, the chapter examines how Gappah’s work reimagines the nation by centring individual trauma, silenced identities and the contested terrain of historical truth.

title: Narratives of Health, Well-Being, and the Zimbabwean Woman's Aesthetic
summary: This chapter explores the intersection of health, well-being, and the Zimbabwean women’s aesthetics through an insightful interview with renowned Zimbabwean author, Valerie Tagwira. The conversation delves into how Tagwira uses narrative to articulate experiences of the body, health, and the socio-political climate, reflecting both personal and collective struggles. Tagwira, known for her keen portrayal of women’s lived realities in contemporary Zimbabwe, speaks to how the aesthetic choices in her work serve as a response to both gendered violence and the broader challenges faced by women in post-colonial Africa. The interview discussion focused on how Tagwira, through her two novels, The Uncertainty of Hope (2006) and Trapped (2020) , challenges and redefines national narratives through their representations of health and well-being. title: History and Background of the Traditional Latin Mass
summary: Abstract This chapter provides a foundation for understanding the TLM. It frames the “Tridentine” Mass as a tool of unity that provided a stable liturgical identity for the Church for four centuries. The chapter then explores the mid-twentieth-century Liturgical Movement, which sought to increase active lay participation, setting the stage for the Second Vatican Council. The tension is analyzed between the Council’s official document, Sacrosanctum Concilium, which aimed for moderate reform, and the rapid, sweeping changes that followed, culminating in the 1969 Novus Ordo. The chapter details the emergence of organized resistance, from the aesthetic petitions of cultural luminaries (the “Agatha Christie indult”) to the more radical defiance of Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre and the SSPX. It concludes by examining how Popes John Paul II and Benedict XVI attempted to reconcile “loyal” traditionalists through the creation of the FSSP and the formal recognition of the TLM’s place within the mai...

title: Reinterpretasi Makna Laba: Mengungkap Dimensi Melampaui Materi pada Pengrajin Tenun Buton
summary: Conceptions of profit in accounting are predominantly defined by material-financial dimensions, often overlooking non-material values embedded in traditional economic practices. While previous studies on alternative profit meanings have largely focused on modern Islamic micro-enterprises or agricultural settings, empirical exploration into traditional Indigenous craftspeople particularly within the unique socio-cultural context of Buton remains scarce. This research aims to reveal the meaning of profit from the perspective of traditional woven fabric artisans in Sulaa Village, Baubau City. Employing a qualitative descriptive approach with Edmund Husserl’s transcendental phenomenology, data were collected through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and documentation. Following Husserl’s methodological framework, the data analysis was systematically conducted through four interrelated stages: epoche, phenomenological reduction, eidetic variation, and the synthesis of structural...

title: Introduction
summary: Abstract This chapter introduces Neba Solo and the style of music he plays. It also explains his development of the bass bala, reorganization of solo and accompaniment parts and addition of choreographed dancing. It provides an overview of Mali’s history and music since the Mali Empire, explaining the differences between the music of jelis and that of non-jelis, such as Oumou Sangaré, Boubacar Traoré, Bassekou Kouyate, and Neba Solo. Finally, the chapter explains the four contextualizing themes of the book: Ethnography and Ethnomusicology (including the book’s theoretical perspectives), Music and Song, Mali’s rich precolonial history, and the history of its contemporary political crises.

title: The stories Europeans tell themselves
authors: Catherine E. De Vries, Alexandros Kentikelenis
summary: Abstract This chapter examines how Europeans attach meaning to cooperation on the continent. Rather than assuming a single, settled answer to what ‘Europe’ is, the authors treat it as an ongoing work of interpretation: a label whose content is constantly reworked by governments, parties, courts, scholars, activists, and citizens. There is no timeless definition. What the term evokes depends on the moment, the vantage point, and the people invoking it. For some, Europe is a civilizational project; for others, a market, a legal order, a security community, or a distant bureaucracy. There are many Europes, coexisting and overlapping. The chapter reconstructs the post-war Union’s most durable master narratives—peace, prosperity, and rules-bound freedom—as a shifting meta-story about what the EU is for and how it survives, without reading history backwards as if these meanings were inevitable. Instead, the chapter traces how narratives were assembled, repackaged, and contested in real time,...

title: Dancing on the Margins
summary: Abstract An intellectual memoir, or autobiography, intersects life events, people, and reading, and in the case of political psychology also the contemporary world on which we are expected to reflect. Over a career’s decades scholars change, as does the field—what is important, how to address it? This chapter identifies four phases in Helen Haste’s life of scholarship. First she explored the development of moral reasoning. Via activism around gender, she moved to research on how language, metaphor, and narrative are inherent to social change, and to exploring cultural processes more broadly. Her ongoing focus has been on youth civic participation and civic education—how to create effective, active citizens. Increasingly she is preoccupied with social change and its unpredictability, disruption, and uncertainty—and what this means for education.

title: Of Entanglements and Intersections
summary: This chapter examines the entanglement and intersection of masculinities, ethnicity and race in the (re)imagining of the Zimbabwean nation in Irene Sabatini’s The Boy Next Door . It contents that as nations are often imagined as male constructs, a gyno-centric (re)reading of the dynamics of masculinities and their intersections and entanglements with other aspects of identity such as race, ethnicity and femininities in the national body-politic is critical in understanding and (re-) imagining Zimbabwean national identities along the continuum of its history from the colonial era to the present as well as future ones. So, the narration of the nation by a female writer via a female protagonist can destabilise its traditional phallo-centricity and also reveal its fissures and recover some of the unsavoury aspects of its history that are at the core of the (re)imagination of the national consciousness.

title: Rewriting the Unfinished Nation
summary: A nation lives in the voices and memories it honours, the truths it buries, and the histories that remain only in absence. Zimbabwean women’s writing constitutes a profoundly contested site of narrative authority, controversy, and recovery. When women narrate Zimbabwe, they unsettle its terms of legibility and interrogate the exclusionary narratives from which belonging is authorised. These writers reposition embodiment, memory, and relational responsibility as the very grammar of national intelligibility. Their fictional works depict colonial rule, nationalist patriarchy, ethnic violence, and postcolonial precarity as entangled regimes of power that determine which lives are tellable and which suffering enters national history. This chapter advances the central claim of this volume with renewed urgency: Zimbabwean women’s literature functions as a counter-archive, critical method, and ethical provocation, making the nation legible through fracture over proclamation. From Vera’s inscri...

title: Desire in Modern European Philosophy
summary: The nature of desire, the way in which it is distinct from other mental states, and the role it plays in action (to name just a few central topics) are common subjects of discussion in Modern European philosophy. In fact, topics such as these are so prevalent in this cultural and temporal period that one could easily fill the pages of a handbook devoted solely to the topic of this chapter. My aim here is therefore the limited one of briefly outlining how a select few seventeenth- and eighteenth-century British and Continental European philosophers understood desire and its role in action and choice. I not only discuss figures who are established members of the Western philosophical canon (such as Locke and Kant in Sections 1 and 4 respectively), but also somewhat lesser-known figures (such as Wolff and Hutcheson in Sections 2 and 3 respectively) who were profoundly influential even though they are read less-often in the present day. Included in each section is a brief discussion of how...

title: Pleasure and Desire
summary: This chapter examines the relationship between pleasure and desire, with special attention to the possibility of reducing pleasure to desire, or desire to pleasure. There are plausible arguments for and against both reductive theories. Some of the arguments appeal to the normative roles of pleasure and desire, but there are also empirical findings from affective neuroscience that are relevant to both theories. One lesson from the discussion is that theorists of different backgrounds have different desiderata for a theory of pleasure or desire, and these competing desiderata push theorists to develop their theories in different directions.

title: Gossart. Architect
summary: This dissertation reconsiders Jan Gossart (d. 1532), conventionally seen as a painter, through the architectural dimensions of his artistic output. Departing from his contemporary designation as both painter and architect, it asks how Gossart negotiated the boundaries between the disciplines and how his designs illuminate the emergence of the architect as an intellectual and creative practitioner in the early sixteenth-century Low Countries. Rather than assessing his works by the architectural dogma codified by the next generation, including Sebastiano Serlio and Pieter Coecke van Aelst, the study recontextualises Gossart's works within a period when the guiding architectural principles were being established. Although they would later define the architectural orders, the language of antiquity was far more fluid and experimental in Gossart's time. Adopting a microhistorical approach, the dissertation combines archival research, a close visual analysis, material-technical investigation ...

title: தமழப பணபடட மரபல வரநதமபல சநதன – ஒர வரலறற நகக: The Concept of Hospitality in Tamil Cultural Tradition: A Historical Perspective
summary: The ancient Tamils were distinguished in culture and civilisation, and their literature shows that they upheld ethical principles in both personal and social life. Hospitality (viruntōmpal) is among the most central of these principles. The Tirukkuṟaḷ (Kural 81) declares that the whole purpose of keeping a household is to cherish guests and to help others. This study examines, from a historical perspective, how Sangam poetry, the Tirukkuṟaḷ, the epics Cilappatikāram and Maṇimēkalai, the Śaiva works Periyapurāṇam and Tirumantiram, other religious traditions and Tamil folk practice portray hospitality. It traces its development from a social obligation within the patron–bard relationship of the Sangam age, to a householder's virtue in the didactic literature, to service of fellow devotees in the bhakti period. It then assesses how urbanisation, nuclear families, lack of time and commercialisation have changed its forms in contemporary society. Using descriptive, comparative and analytica...

title: Holding and unholding the wound: Trauma and the feminine ethics of endurance in Brick Lane
authors: Aafia Shereen, Shantanu Ghosh, Sutapa Dutta
summary: In contemporary times, migration extends beyond its literal meaning of a change in location. It becomes a source of gender discrimination where the experiences of men and those of women differ significantly. Women endure not just the trauma of displacement but also resentment from a restrictive community abroad. This paper investigates Monica Ali’s Brick Lane (2003) as a literary record showing the ways in which trauma is inflicted upon migrant women and how they ultimately come out of its shackles. Drawing on trauma theory and feminist scholarship, this paper probes the insidious nature of trauma that consumes Nazneen, the protagonist of the novel. The analysis extends the discussion by showing how communal judgement and enforced domesticity fracture migrant women’s identity. summary: Mapuche poetry and poetry in Guaraní currently constitute two areas of aesthetic experimentation of special attention for specialised critics. This paper will focus on a corpus that establishes dialogues between both areas: the analysis will focus, mainly but not exclusively, on a work by Adriana Paredes Pinda, a Chilean Mapuche poet; and Pola Gómez Codina, a poet belonging to the generation of the children of Paraguayans in Argentina, in which the Guaraní language enters in different ways. In view of their confluences and specificities, it is of interest to investigate two metaphor-notions emanating from a corpus of literary texts and paratexts, xampurria and jopara, understood in this article as a locus of enunciation. The hypothesis underpinning this research postulates that from this place of enunciation, identity purisms are counteracted by the subversion of the minoritising conception of both concepts. Diaspora, a constitutive experience of these literary zones, has repercussions...

title: Preface
summary: In the fall of 2002, I traveled to northeastern Brazil to teach at a small private school. I stumbled on the opportunity through a family connection: The school’s founder, Jonatas Lima, was a college friend of my aunt’s. Jon spent several Thanksgivings with my family in Maine; I heard my first maxixe in the late 1980s in one of Jon’s spellbinding performances of Nazareth on my grandparents’ upright piano. In 2002, the summer after I graduated from college, I was hoping to teach abroad. He was seeking a long-term substitute to teach intermediate and advanced English and piano lessons. We phoned my aunt the same week. A month later I left to spend four months in Jon’s home with his parents, Pastor David and Dona Iraci, as my hosts in Juazeiro do Norte, Ceará. A ten-hour bus ride from the beachside state capital and into the sertão, the drought-prone Brazilian “backlands,” Juazeiro do Norte sees few American tourists. title: An Arts Immersion Approach in Initial Teacher Education
summary: While pre-service teachers (PSTs) are expected to learn how to teach in complex, diverse and dynamic classrooms, these capabilities are not well developed in PST programs. However, an Arts Immersion approach has been developed as a pedagogical response to the needs of PSTs, in-service teachers, students and schools to resist the dominant transactional pedagogy reflected in lecture formats that position PSTs as passive receptacles of knowledge. An Arts Immersion approach in initial teacher education (ITE) provides different ways of knowing for PSTs to co-create knowledge by using the shared creative and embodied languages of the arts. Evidence is drawn from two research projects conducted in Queensland primary schools, demonstrating how an Arts Immersion approach can overcome barriers, deepen understanding and foster a joy in the learning process. This chapter demonstrates how an Arts Immersion pedagogy explicitly builds the capacities PSTs need to develop a relational, responsive and r...

Polish women artists had thus entered the dynamically evolving sphere of modern art. Through close textual analysis, the study examines Yeong-hye's vegetarianism, silence, bodily withdrawal, and vegetal transformation in relation to theories of agency and relational ethics. Drawing on Saba Mahmood's reconceptualization of agency, Carol J. Adams's ecofeminist critique of the interconnected oppression of women, animals, and nature, and Talal Asad's critique of secular intelligibility, the article advances a central argument: that the novel stages an irresolvable double movement between psychological pathology and ethical becoming, refusing to subordinate either possibility to the other. This argument is developed most fully through Yeong-hye's vegetal transformation...
