title: Le boeuf sur le toit and Milhaud’s Transnational Latinité
summary: Abstract Darius Milhaud’s Le boeuf sur le toit has historically been read as an exoticist meditation on (Black) Brazilian difference, but this chapter situates the work’s origins instead in elite discourses in both France and Brazil that sought to highlight commonality rather than difference by emphasizing a shared “Latin” character and heritage. Milhaud blurred the lines between a French “Self” and a Brazilian “Other” strategically through this rhetoric of shared latinité. This discourse served both the wartime supranationalist French propaganda he was charged with disseminating and elite Brazilian efforts that sought to align Brazil—both culturally and racially—with “Latinness” rather than Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous peoples. Discourses of shared latinité reflected Milhaud’s experiences as a Provençal, in wartime propaganda efforts, and as a participant in Rio de Janeiro’s elite, Francophile arts scene. Milhaud’s interest in French regionalism, French nationalism, and supranational...

title: Innocence by Accreditation: Mythic Branding and Audit Feminism in Athena Swan
summary: Abstract The UK’s Athena Swan Charter positions itself as a policy instrument, an award-based scheme for improving gender equality through self-assessment, evidence gathering, and action planning. I argue that this description overlooks the fact that Athena Swan is also a semiotic framework that governs gender through naming, iconography, and the public performance of institutional virtue. I defend three claims. First, the Charter’s mythic-inflected branding, acronym, and iconography frame the ideal of intelligible, respectable gender-equality practice that is in tension with emancipatory aims of loosening coercive gender norms and challenging credibility hierarchies. Second, insofar as Athena Swan operates by conferring public credentials, I elucidate how its semiotics function not merely expressively but also as instruments of legitimation that shape incentives, trust, institutional identity, and the handling of dissent. Third, I contend that the Charter’s credential economy is suppo...

summary: Abstract Chapter 1 provides guidance for the reader by alluring them to focus on observation, that is, to perceive and reflect on what is happening in this very moment and place in the text and context as well as between the reader and the book. This chapter also calls for accepting ‘we’ as a collective enactor, a unit of analysis, despite the problems related to its vagueness. title: The ELIZA Effect: Why Machines That Talk Like People Should Still Be Treated as Machines
summary: A computer asks how you feel. You describe a personal problem. It responds sympathetically, remembers something you mentioned earlier and formulates a question that seems unusually perceptive. After several exchanges, it no longer feels as though you are operating software. It feels as though someone—or something—is listening.That feeling is the essence of the ELIZA effect: the human tendency to attribute understanding, emotion, intention, personality or consciousness to a computer system because its behavior displays the outward signs normally associated with a mind.

summary: This response to Douglas Moggach's recent book Freedom and Perfection: German Political Thought from Leibniz to Marx discusses its compelling argumentative thread, in which Leibnizian perfectionism is redefined and reframed in the thought of Kant and his successors in German political thought. Moggach's analysis is briefly examined in relation to depictions of China in Enlightenment and post-Enlightenment political thought, including that of Leibniz, Wolff, Kant, Herder, and Hegel. Kant's historical teleology, as developed in his Critique of Judgement and select essays, is curiously under-emphasized in Moggach's book. title: Conduits of Wisdom
summary: Despite a Pauline tradition against women teaching men and an assumption that they were easy prey for false teachers (I Timothy 5. 13‒16), evidence from the second to fourth century Gnostic and Valentinian texts suggests that women could be counted as ‘spiritually enlightened’ teachers. Along with familiar male apostles, a tradition of ‘the seven’ women followers who can teach the true meaning of Jesus’s words surfaces in Gnostic revelation dialogues. Ptolemy, a second-century Valentinian teacher in Rome, extended the possibility of advanced instruction to a woman, Flora. Stories that depict Jesus intervening when male apostles attempt to silence women, especially Mary Magdalene, reflect continual tensions over women as conduits of Jesus’s authentic teaching.

title: The Lost Species because of Its Fear of Nature
summary: Abstract Chapter 8 portrays the problem in existence with a diagnosis technique, eco-phenomenosophy, to search for remedies to the existential condition of being lost. It discovers the roots of the crisis and an eternity of misperception in the relationship between humans and nature. Humans are claimed to be afraid of both their external and internal nature. And because of this fear, naturaphobia, the species and its cultures have sought to abandon nature. We have become disorientated because we do not know what nature is and where it is anymore. This has led us to postmodernism and to fighting with our own shadows of which eco-fascism is treated as an example.

title: Toen dichters blaften: Romantiek, rebellie en literaire underground in het Delft van de jaren tachtig
summary: Dit artikel reconstrueert de ontwikkeling van een kleinschalige, onafhankelijke literaire subcultuur in Delft gedurende de jaren tachtig. Centraal staan jonge dichters, alternatieve publicaties en culturele initiatieven die zich grotendeels buiten de gevestigde literaire instellingen bewogen. Aan de hand van oorspronkelijke tijdschriften, programmamateriaal, eigentijdse krantenberichten en persoonlijke herinneringen wordt de geschiedenis belicht van onder meer Het Romantisch Collectief, De Jonge Honden van Delft, het literaire katern Vlam en Stichting Kultus. Bijzondere aandacht gaat uit naar de romantisch-existentiële opvattingen van deze dichters, hun zoektocht naar artistieke onafhankelijkheid en de wisselwerking tussen poëzie, performance en experimentele kunst. Ook de Delftse Nacht van de Poëzie (1986), het poëziefestival Delft dicht (1988) en de bredere ontwikkeling van de alternatieve Delftse cultuur komen aan bod. Het artikel beoogt geen uitputtende geschiedschrijving te bieden...

summary: This article introduces a theoretical framework for art-based ecocultural animation and develops a practice-oriented model within the context of Arctic art and culture. The study draws on theories of sociocultural animation, community-based art education, and ecoculture, as well as the authors’ long-term action research conducted in northern environments. Ecocultural animation aims to support the development of ecocultural understanding and agency. Art-based ecocultural animation is conceptualized as a process in which ecological, cultural, communal, and artistic dimensions are interwoven in a transformative way. Ecosystems, seasonal cycles, and more-than-human environments are understood as active participants shaping relationships, meanings, and practices. The model supports the emergence and impact of long- term, locally grounded ecocultural practices, offering a concrete and hopeful approach to addressing ecological and cultural challenges. title: Unlocking the Legacy of Memnon: creative resources for teaching the Ethiopian hero – a joint NCLG–ACL project
summary: Abstract Memnon, a demigod, a Homeric hero, and a wise and fearless King of Ethiopia, appeared in many ancient Greek and Latin texts. Memnon was a key ally who came to the aid of King Priam of Troy and met his end in the Trojan War in a duel with Achilles, as Zeus, Thetis, and Eos looked on. Recently, a new play about Memnon was written by Will Power and produced by the Classical Theatre of Harlem under Director Carl Cofield at The J. Paul Getty Museum in California and at the Classical Theatre of Harlem’s venues in New York City. In this article, I will describe both the process and the resulting open-access teaching resources created by the National Committee for Latin and Greek in a joint project with the American Classical League in response to this new play, Memnon . Integral to our efforts is a call for continued collaboration with colleagues to help advance our goal of creating many more classroom-ready resources.

title: THE ROLE OF HISTORICAL COSTUMES IN CONTEMPORARY FASHION
summary: This article analyzes the role of historical costumes in the development of contemporary fashion, their influence on the design and garment creation process, and the ways in which elements of historical clothing appear in modern fashion trends. Historical costumes are important works of art that reflect the cultural heritage, aesthetic views, social status, and lifestyles of different peoples. Contemporary designers combine tradition and innovation by incorporating cuts, fabrics, ornaments, colors, and silhouettes characteristic of historical periods. The article examines the influence of costumes from antiquity, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and the nineteenth and twentieth centuries on contemporary fashion. It also highlights the importance of historical heritage in preserving cultural traditions, promoting national values, and developing the principles of sustainable fashion.

title: Securitizing the Fences of Capital: Disposability, Racialized Border Regimes, and Absurdity as Critique in Gianna Molinari’s Hier ist noch alles möglich
summary: Gianna Molinari’s 2018 novel Hier ist noch alles möglich is set in a Swiss factory approaching closure, narrated by a night watchwoman whose repetitive patrols along the fences defamiliarize borders and surveillance by making them visible as practices enmeshed in regimes of capital accumulation. At a time of mass redundancies, policing the factory’s fences in its dying days becomes an allegory of modes of securing the stability of capital during crisis times. I read Molinari’s allegorical aesthetics as illuminating how controlling people who are about to be rendered surplus goes hand-in-hand with displacement onto a racialized crisis of borders. Textual figuration of avoiding dealing with the root causes of surplusification emphasises the question about what has the capacity to render people disposable. title: A study of Chen Xiaoqi's music creation: a literature-based review of its developmental trajectory and characteristics
summary: Chen Xiaoqi is a representative and influential songwriter in the development of contemporary Chinese popular music. His creative career has spanned the various historical stages since the launch of China's reform and opening-up, yet systematic academic research on his work remains relatively underdeveloped. Chen Xiaoqi holds a pioneering position in the creation of Chinese-style popular songs, and his "Southern School" artistic style has exerted a profound influence on popular music in mainland China. Through a systematic review of existing literature and historical materials, this study aims to clarify the trajectory of Chen Xiaoqi's creative development, the artistic characteristics of different stages of his career, and the reasons underlying his success. title: FROM OBSERVATION TO RESISTANCE: THE EMERGENCE OF A NEW CONSCIOUSNESS IN BAMA'S THE ICHI TREE MONKEY
summary: Bama is a significant author in Dalit literature today. The focus of these narratives is on the hardships and everyday lives of Dalits. She writes on the topic related to social exclusion, labour, poverty, gender inequality and caste prejudice. N. Ravi Shankar’s English translation of her short story, The Ichi Tree Monkey, seems to be a straightforward account of rural life. Other topics like human behaviour, societal views, childhood, tradition, empathy and awareness are covered, nevertheless. Parvathi and her bond with the ichi tree are the primary subjects of the narrative. From her early years into her adulthood, this friendship persisted. The monkey that is associated with the tree is crucial to the narrative. Bama illustrates how people’s perceptions of nature and animals may shift via the monkey. title: Learning and Belonging in Les Demeurées: A Semiotic Reading of Educational Authority and Intellectual Emancipation
summary: Jeanne Benameur’s Les Demeurées presents learning as a conflict over what knowledge does to relationships. This article examines how the novella constructs that conflict through recurrent semantic features, competing narrative programmes, and changes in the modalities of learning. A close reading of the French text combines Greimassian narrative semiotics with Rastierian interpretive semantics; Rancière’s account of intellectual emancipation provides a subsequent philosophical perspective. The analysis identifies a discrepancy between Luce’s retention of school discourse and her refusal to display or appropriate it under conditions associated with separation from her mother. Recurrent figures of enclosure, thresholds, naming, and material inscription change function as educational authority shifts. Embroidery reconnects retained lessons with bodily attention and an emerging wish to address the teacher. Yet this transformation neither vindicates withdrawal from schooling nor establishes...

title: The post-Yugoslav subject: Mobility, liminality, and post-war trauma in Goran Vojnović’s novel Jugoslavija, moja dežela (Yugoslavia, My Fatherland)
summary: The article focuses on the novel Jugoslavija, moja dežela ( Yugoslavia, My Fatherland ) by the Slovenian author Goran Vojnović, one of the key works of post-Yugoslav literature, combining reflection on migration in the territory of the former Yugoslavia with an analysis of the crisis of identity following the violent dissolution of the political community. The study explores the individual experience of migration as a reflection of a broader generational condition, as well as a form of spatial mobility that alternately emerges as necessity and as a quest – for the father, for identity, for the recovery of memory, and for confronting post-war trauma. It argues that migration is not merely a thematic concern of the novel, but a structuring principle that shapes its narrative architecture, spatial configuration, and construction of subjectivity. The protagonist is portrayed as a hybrid, transnational, liminal figure who moves between non-places, negotiating the meaning of homeland/fatherl...

title: Caste, Gender, and Subaltern Agency: A Sociological Analysis of Kainli Kamini’s Resistance in Nepal
summary: Yogmaya Neupane is increasingly recognized as an important woman reformer who challenged caste discrimination, gender inequality, religious orthodoxy, and social injustice in early twentieth-century Nepal. However, marginalized women associated with her movement, particularly Kainli Kamini, remain comparatively invisible in historical and sociological scholarship. Her fragmented historical presence provides an important lens for examining caste, gender, subalternity, agency, resistance, and historical memory. This study critically examines Kainli Kamini’s caste-gender intersectionality and everyday resistance within Yogmaya Neupane’s movement and explores how dominant historical narratives have marginalized or silenced Dalit women’s voices in Nepal. The study adopts a qualitative historical-sociological approach based on documentary analysis, textual interpretation, and subaltern feminist reading. title: E(co): An exploration of ecological musicking through live electro-acoustic music practice
summary: This doctoral study investigates how live electro-acoustic music practice can be reimagined through ecological and posthumanist perspectives, approached through a reflexive inquiry into my own artistic practice. Motivated by concerns over the cultural conditions in which music is currently made, shared, and understood - marked by hyper-individualism, ecological detachment, the commodification of creativity, and the rise of generative AI fabrications - this research positions ecological musicking as a situated, practice-led response. Rather than proposing a fixed methodology or style, it offers an alternative ethos of composing, performing, and listening that foregrounds interdependence, relationality, and responsiveness. While ecological themes have been explored in music and sound art, they are often treated as content rather than as a structural principle embedded in practice. This thesis addresses that gap by reframing musicking as an entangled, relational activity that unfolds thro...

title: Spaces of encounter: public art & Black spatial aesthetics
summary: This dissertation asks a deceptively simple question: How does public space feel to Black inhabitants? In the United States, urban environments are often treated as neutral containers—designed to be efficient, legible, and orderly. Yet for Black communities, space has rarely been neutral. The built environment has been shaped by racialized policy, spatial exclusion, and aesthetic regimes that render Black life peripheral, disposable, or out of place. Streets, walls, facades, and public artworks do not merely decorate cities; they condition perception, behavior, and belonging through repeated encounters. This project begins from the premise that aesthetic environments shape life chances. What we see, touch, move through, and repeatedly encounter trains perception over time—shaping orientation, expectation, and felt possibility. Increasingly, research across environmental psychology, public health, and neuroscience suggests that the built environment plays a role in nervous system regula...

title: Integrating multistylistic influences in a portfolio of compositions
summary: This thesis examines how I have integrated multistylistic influences into a portfolio of nine compositions. The composition portfolio contains a body of work for a variety of instrumental combinations, including individual instruments, a piano quintet and a large-scale ensemble piece. A description of how my compositions reside within the framework of composers who operate in similar styles and influences is presented, followed by a commentary on individual pieces in the portfolio of compositions. The accompanying commentary then discusses four main research areas. Firstly, I discuss the development of my compositional style, from early musical experience with the accordion and Scottish traditional music, to classical piano training, and my subsequent interest in jazz. A further three research areas are then explored in relation to my process of composition. I examine my use of rhythmic devices common to the jazz and classical idioms such as polymetrics, and I discuss the use of improv...

According to the French Institute's description, the work is considered a comedy and musical fiction, running for 1 hour and 26 minutes, which tells the story of Hombre, a dance teacher in Abidjan who formed Ensemble Koteba with talented young artists. The argument presented is that film can become a particularly rich educational tool thanks to its composition of diverse semiotic systems—image, speech, music, dance, gesture, space, and narrative—and its capacity to simultaneously develop linguistic, cultur...

title: Forest shadows: analysis of select marimba works by Robert Paterson
summary: In the existent academic discourse, the solo marimba music of Robert Paterson (b. 1970) has yet to be thoroughly examined. Existing literature passes over the contributions of Paterson with only a handful of cursory acknowledgements. Though he has many works that use percussion extensively, including works for marimba plus one instrument, a large-scale, multi-movement work for marimba with choir, and several percussion ensembles, this monograph focuses on Paterson’s contribution and style within the marimba solo literature. Selected works discussed include Komodo (1998, revised 2004) and Forest Shadows (2011). Through these detailed analyses, this monograph paints a more complete picture of Paterson’s compositional language and contributions to the solo marimba literature and offers greater awareness and context to these deserving works.

title: Hegel's negative aesthetics
summary: This dissertation develops an interpretation of what I call Hegel’s “negative aesthetics,” the systematic account of art as the sensuous presentation of spirit understood as negativity. On my reading, art is not a presentation that makes spirit transparent to itself, but an activity whose constitutive condition is a structural gap between the artwork as spirit’s externalization (Entäußerung) and the content it purports to express. This gap is an immanent limit of artistic presentation as such: the sensuous form that spirit externalizes itself into is, by virtue of being sensuous, always already inadequate to what it is supposed to present. This immanent inadequacy grounds Hegel’s dual claims about the end of art and the end of beauty—the joint proclamation that beauty is impossible in modernity, ushering art’s loss of vocation— as necessary moments internal to art’s own logic as a form of absolute spirit. My dissertation takes seriously Hegel’s core metaphysical claim that spirit is th...

title: ‘Being there’ in a story world: an explication of narrative presence
summary: Marvin Minsky (1980) first introduced “telepresence,” a high-quality simulation-based teleoperation system that allows remote workers to experience a sense of ‘being there’ at a physical workplace. (tele)Presence provides technology users with a mediated experience in which they feel “a sense of being there,” as if they are experiencing the ‘natural’ physical environment (Lombard & Ditton, 1997). Although the concept of presence has been widely discussed as a sensation experienced during VR use (Riva, Mantovani, Waterworth & Waterworth, 2015), as research has expanded, there has been a growing scholarly debate over a theoretical conundrum regarding the nature of presence and its medium. How can we explain why a book, a century-old form of media, can produce such a rich, immersive experience? This dissertation proposes a theoretical solution to the ‘book problem’ by redefining narrative presence. title: Ruined and rebuilt: constructing the ideal baroque city after natural disasters
summary: This dissertation addresses the effects of natural disasters on urban planning and architecture in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in Italy and Iberia, and more broadly as a colonial phenomenon, as in the Philippines. Responses to natural disasters, varying by administration and local conditions, led to the evolution of architectural building practices and techniques, centering the term “Earthquake Baroque.” A focus of this project is on how architects implemented the idealization of the cityscape following calamitous events. The ideals of eighteenth-century city planning had their origin in sixteenth-century humanist and architectural writing as well as seen in the actual cities that provided models, notably Rome and Madrid. Different ideal plans were created for port cities, regions, and imperial cities, such as Manila, Philippines (1645), Val di Noto, Sicily (1693), and Lisbon, Portugal (1755), immediately after natural disasters caused major civic disruption.Disasters, esp...

title: Searching for drawings in sixteenth-century Italy: provenances and networking in the eye of the collector
summary: This dissertation examines the circulation of drawings as autonomous works of art in sixteenth-century Italy and traces the development of a market for the medium. Beginning in the sixteenth century, drawings came to be appreciated more broadly as works of art in their own right, leading to an increased demand for the medium among collectors. As their status changed, drawings also began to be perceived as commodities that could be exchanged not only through practices of gift-giving and bartering but also through direct monetary transactions. Through an analysis of primary sources, including letters, inventories, and notary documents, this study reconstructs the main resources employed by collectors to obtain drawings for their collections and explores the complex social dynamics that contributed to the emergence of a market for the medium. The figure of the Florentine collector Niccolò Gaddi (1537–1591), who gathered one of the largest collections of the late sixteenth century, exempli...

title: Reading aguajes: spiritual manifestations and subtextual disruptions in diasporic Caribbean literature
summary: This dissertation develops aguajes as a critical framework for reading contemporary diasporic Caribbean literature, conceptualizing them as subtextual and spiritual manifestations that interrupt hegemonic distinctions between the material and the immaterial, the visible and the unseen. Drawing from Afro-Caribbean epistemologies, familial memory, and linguistic registers rooted in Puerto Rican usage, aguajes are understood as moments of perceptual disruption through which suppressed histories, ancestral presences, and embodied knowledges emerge into narrative form. Moving from the intimate domestic space of Angie Cruz’s Soledad, to the diasporic and sensory terrain of Elizabeth Acevedo’s Clap When You Land, and finally to the urban and collective dimensions of Daniel José Older’s Shadowshaper and Alexis C. Garcia’s Daughter of the Sea, this project traces how aguajes expand from localized manifestations into broader modes of cultural memory and creative recovery. The project is structur...

title: Illustrating the lives of the prophets in sixteenth-century Islamic manuscripts
summary: This dissertation investigates the representation of Abrahamic prophets in a wide range of illustrated manuscripts produced throughout the Ottoman and Safavid empires in the sixteenth century. The large number of manuscripts in Istanbul and the worldwide collections illustrating the lives of the prophets attests to the investment in commissioning and collecting such works. I explore how manuscripts illustrating the tales of the prophets lead the reader, viewer, or listener to experience these miraculous stories through four overarching themes. I comparatively analyze the visual language and symbolisms in the tales of the prophets, a collection of stories found not only in hagiographies but across books of many genres including universal histories, mystical romances, scientific treatises, and anthologies of poetry. In each case, the narrative images of the sacred figures conveyed multiple meanings at once, depending on the moral lesson of the story, the genre of the book, and the social...

title: Essays on identity, disclosure, and engagement in the creator economy
summary: Digital platforms increasingly shape how users interpret, support, and engage with creators, communities, and artificial intelligence agents. In the creator economy, engagement is not driven only by content quality, platform functionality, or technical performance. It is also shaped by identity signals embedded in platform tools, creator actions, and AI-mediated interactions. These signals influence how users understand who or what they are engaging with, what the interaction represents, and whether the experience matches their expectations. This dissertation develops an expectation-matching framework for understanding identity-based engagement in digital platforms. The central argument is that identity signals strengthen engagement when they align with users' expectations about a creator, community, or digital actor, but weaken engagement when they dilute, complicate, or violate those expectations. Drawing on empirical evidence from prosocial platform tools and virtual influencer mark...

title: More than the narrative: Black manhood, family, and community
summary: This dissertation examines the evolving construct of Black manhood in America by exploring how the historical memory of Ancient Afrikan traditions serves as a foundation for contemporary understandings of manhood among Black men. Through a cultural and historical analysis, this study argues that Black manhood has consistently served as a site of resistance, self-expression, and communal responsibility, shaped by both cultural practices and the fight against racism. The research begins by delving into Ancient Afrikan manhood, which is defined by spiritual harmony, communal care, self-mastery, and moral integrity. Specifically, it examines how cultural ideals rooted in ancient Afrikan concepts of manhood—such as spiritual harmony, communal responsibility, self-mastery, and moral integrity—have influenced the ways Black men understand and express manhood in the context of American racial oppression. Through cultural and historical analysis, this study traces the transformation of these id...

title: The Representations of Community in The Wandering Earth 2
summary: As one of the representative Chinese science fiction films, released on January 22nd , 2023, The Wandering Earth 2, is adapted from the eponymous novel by a well-known Chinese science fiction writer Cixin Liu. It reveals how human beings across the world overcome countless hardships and obstacles by virtue of collective wisdom, courage and sacrifice, when faced with a truly cataclysmic galactic-level crisis. Given that the “images of community” permeate and run through the entire film, drawing on the community theory proposed by Ferdinand Tönnies, this study has conducted a comprehensive analysis of the representations of community in this film from three dimensions, namely the blood community, the neighborhood community and the spiritual community, so as to examine the necessity and inevitability of a community with a shared future for mankind and justify why “human courage and perseverance shall be engraved forever beneath the stars”.

title: Om-kara As an Integrated Ethnoscience Through Ethnocosmology, Ethnoanatomy and Ethnobioacoustics
summary: The sacred script of Om-kara in Balinese Hindu culture represents a traditional knowledge system encompassing cosmology, anatomy, and bioacoustics. This study analyzes Om-kara through an integrated ethnoscience perspective, connecting Balinese philosophical teachings with contemporary scientific knowledge. Employing qualitative library research, the study applies hermeneutic analysis to Siwa Tattwa, Kadyatmikan, Mantra, and Usada manuscripts, supported by literature on neuroscience, bioacoustics, and medical physiology. The findings reveal three interconnected dimensions. First, ethnocosmologically, Nada and Windu within Ulu Candra symbolize cosmic creation (Utpatti), from Niskala to Prakreti. title: Body Narratives and Identity Construction in Asian Performance Art across Cultural Contexts
summary: Asian performance art has become increasingly visible in transnational exhibition circuits, yet scholarship on it remains divided between single-artist monographs and region-bound surveys, leaving few instruments for reading such work comparatively across the contexts in which it is received. This article proposes the concept of double legibility: the performing body in cross-cultural circulation must signify at once within a local semiotic economy of ritual, kinship, language and historical memory, and within a transnational curatorial economy that has inherited habits of reading Asian bodies as ethnographic evidence. The body carries inherited material of its own; what the two regimes govern is not whether that material exists but what it is taken to mean. Identity in this situation is produced relationally, in the distance between the two readings. title: Hidden Networks and Secret Exports:Lucien and Alexandrine Bonaparte’s London Sales
summary: The dispersal of the antiquities excavated at Vulci by Lucien and Alexandrine Bonaparte is generally thought to have begun with the Paris auctions of the 1830s, while the Campanari family are credited with pioneering the exhibition and sale of Etruscan antiquities in London. Drawing on correspondence, newspaper reports, advertisements, and archival material, this article shows that the Bonapartes were exporting antiquities to England from 1829 and organising exhibitions and sales in London from 1830, earlier than previously recognised. It reconstructs the networks that enabled these activities, highlighting the roles of Alexandrine Bonaparte and female intermediaries including Letizia Bonaparte Wyse, Christine Bonaparte Stuart, and Anna Maria Gordon. summary: Abstract Henrik Ibsen’s A Doll’s House (1879), a landmark play, has an important place in the development of modern drama. Nora Helmer is the protagonist and her expedition from punctual domestication to alert personal freedom represents the declaration of individuality against conventional patriarchy. This study finds Ibsen as a social critic and an ethical dramatist and tries to expose the functional boundaries in traditional domestic life drawing upon Gail Finney’s Ibsen and Feminism and The Second Sex by Simone de Beauvoir. The transformation of Nora excels the personal and it embodies a universal challenge. The significance of this play lies in restructuring the female protagonist who is very passive and stereotyped, asserts the self and crosses the narrow constraints. title: Rethinking Roland Barthes's "The Death of the Author" in Contemporary Media
summary: Abstract This study explores the theoretical transition from structuralism to post-structuralism by examining the current digital system. It applies Roland Barthes’s iconic 1967 concept, ‘The Death of the Author’, directly to modern internet culture. By combining structural linguistics with hyperreality theory, the paper investigates how online meaning is actively generated. It closely analyzes the role of Barthes's the ‘scriptor’ within automated web platform. The research specifically tracks this text transformation across music remixes, short videos, reels, and internet memes. The paper highlights the way corporate platform algorithms systematically tape messages from historical context. When origins disappear, online copies completely replace the original media. Basically, these apps give regular users the freedom to remix and reshare anything they see online. Because of this, everyday media consumers have become the actual writers of modern text."

summary: This research offers new materialist ecofeminist reading of Pearl S. Buck’s The Good Earth. This study combines ecofeminist perspectives with the new materialist approach to examine how the novel, The Good Earth portrays human and non-human entities, highlighting a diffused agency that challenges patriarchal dominance. It contributes to a broader discourse on sustainability, gender justice, and socio-ecological equity. title: Holding and unholding the wound: Trauma and the feminine ethics of endurance in Brick Lane
authors: Aafia Shereen, Shantanu Ghosh, Sutapa Dutta
summary: In contemporary times, migration extends beyond its literal meaning of a change in location. It becomes a source of gender discrimination where the experiences of men and those of women differ significantly. Women endure not just the trauma of displacement but also resentment from a restrictive community abroad. This paper investigates Monica Ali’s Brick Lane (2003) as a literary record showing the ways in which trauma is inflicted upon migrant women and how they ultimately come out of its shackles. title: Ukrainian Art History: Working Through Uncertainties
summary: Ukrainian art history has been shaped by successive waves of political disruption, which affected both the objects available for study and the infrastructures and institutions through which knowledge was produced. Taking the Ukrainian context as a starting point, this conference asks how art history can engage with fragmented archives, contested cultural memory, under-documented artistic practices, and forms of knowledge that exceed institutional frameworks.

title: THE ROLE OF INDIAN KNOWLEDGE TRADITION IN PERSONALITY DEVELOPMENT AND CHARACTER BUILDING
summary: The Indian knowledge tradition (Bharatiya Gyan Parampara) is one of the world’s most ancient and comprehensive systems of wisdom, encompassing philosophy, spirituality, ethics, and education. It provides a holistic framework for the development of human personality and the building of moral character. In an era where personality development is often confined to communication skills and outward behavior, the Indian tradition emphasizes the cultivation of inner consciousness, self-discipline, moral integrity, and service to humanity. This research paper explores the philosophical, spiritual, and educational dimensions of the Indian knowledge tradition and analyzes its relevance in shaping personality and character in contemporary society.

title: Iron-clad Bodies, Fluid Beings. An Idea-Historical Approach to Queer and Posthuman Bodies in Medievalist (Roleplaying) Games
summary: This chapter presents an idea-historical approach to queer and posthuman bodies and embodiment within medievalist roleplaying games (RPGs) through the lens of medieval literature, such as hagiographies. The focus is here set specifically on medievalist games, which do not feature deliberately designed queer characters, but rather exhibit similar features to medieval literature. Locating parallel narratives, features, and concepts between the historical and contemporary, this chapter functions as an introduction to the potential of idea-historical approaches for analysing the role of non-normative bodies in digital medievalist games and contributes to the understanding of intersections between medievalist imaginaries and medieval literature. By offering a dedicated premodern perspective, this chapter offers an extension of the existing posthuman discourses in game studies, which can be more useful for – but is not limited to – the analysis of digital games with historical themes.

title: Moving images, moved audiences? A focus group study into audience interpretations of distant suffering in The Impossible (2012)
authors: Valerie Vanhove, Stijn Joye, David Ongenaert
summary: While distant suffering has been thoroughly explored in factual media such as news and documentaries, this article examines Western audiences’ interpretations of distant suffering and non-Western ‘Others’ in the format of fiction films. Through five focus groups ( N = 22) in Flanders, the northern Dutch-speaking part of Belgium, this explorative study examines whether the film The Impossible (2012) fosters empathy, raises awareness and encourages action towards the portrayed distant suffering. The film tells the story of a British family during the tsunami of 2004 and is largely based on true events. Findings show that the film proves effective in increasing Western viewers’ awareness of distant suffering. However, this sense of closeness mostly resulted in passivity and rarely translated into concrete action. A proper distance from the portrayed Other appears crucial for Western viewers to be motivated to show compassion and consider action. Nevertheless, the study also suggests that ...

title: GOTHIC SPATIALITY AND THE POETICS OF SETTING IN SUSAN HILL’S THE WOMAN IN BLACK
authors: Nataliia Banias, Kateryna Lizak, Daniela Vashkeba
summary: The article examines the representation and functions of Gothic space in Susan Hill’s novel “The Woman in Black” (1983), focusing on the relationship between spatial organization, atmosphere, narrative tension, and the supernatural. The study argues that setting in Hill’s novel should not be regarded merely as a passive background against which the events unfold. Instead, geographical, architectural, domestic, and natural spaces actively participate in the construction of Gothic meaning and shape the protagonist’s psychological experience. Particular attention is paid to Eel Marsh House, the surrounding marshes, the causeway, the village of Crythin Gifford, London, and the recurring motifs of fog, water, darkness, isolation, and restricted visibility. Eel Marsh House is analysed as a central Gothic locus in which domestic space is transformed into an uncanny and hostile environment. The marshes and the sea further destabilize the opposition between land and water, safety and danger, fa...

title: Poetry and drama: changing fortunes, 1650–1900
summary: Abstract The period from the mid-17th to the mid-18th century is rightly thought of as the pre-eminent age of satire in Europe, especially in France and England. It produced both theorists and major practitioners of the genre, including Molière, Voltaire, Dryden, and Pope, who are still read today. Targets were plentiful. The old abuses and corruptions continued and wars abounded, but the new developments in philosophy and natural knowledge known as the Enlightenment created new topics for ridicule. Molière and Voltaire mocked the state of learning from different perspectives. Dryden and Pope developed the dominant vehicle for verse satire, the heroic couplet, but it coexisted with more jocular metres and irreverent styles. Drama was formally inventive and so outspoken against the government that it was censored from 1738. During the period of Romanticism and revolution, satire was a weapon for both radicals and conservatives. Satirical poetry declined somewhat in the 19th century, tho...

title: Star Wars at Fifty
authors: Patrick B. Sharp, Mihaela Mihailova, Jason W. Ellis, David Shipko, Andrew Shephard, Christina Lord, Leigh Edwards, De Witt Kilgore, Sohini Sarah Pillai, Frederick Luis Aldama
summary: This symposium celebrates the 50th anniversary of Star Wars (1977) with nineteen short essays from scholars who discuss its meaning, impact, and legacy. The essays examine the migrations and manifestations of the Star Wars universe across media, including animation, video games, novels, comics, collectibles, and television. The scholars in this symposium explore topics such as race, ethnicity, sexuality, fandom, artificial intelligence, and animals in Star Wars texts.

title: An Analytical and Descriptive Examination of the Wisdoms and Secrets of the Phenomenon of Repetition in the Holy Qur’an
authors: Rana Vahdani Banam, Hossein Moradi Zanjani, Mohammad hosein Saeini
summary: The phenomenon of repetition in the Holy Qur’an is among the significant and longstanding subjects in Qur’anic studies and the science of exegesis. Despite the attention given by some exegetes and scholars to the nature and underlying wisdoms of repetition, this issue still requires independent and more in-depth investigation. This necessity arises because many viewpoints on the subject have been presented only sporadically or implicitly, leaving a noticeable research gap in its systematic examination. In this regard, the approach of Allameh Tabataba’i, as a distinguished contemporary Qur’anic exegete, deserves particular attention due to its methodological and ijtihād-based nature. Employing a descriptive-analytical method, the present study examines his perspectives as articulated in Tafsir al-Mizan and succeeds in identifying more than twenty wisdoms and functions of repetition in the Qur’an. The findings indicate that repetition in the Qur’an is by no means redundant; rather, it is...

title: Well-being in digital-free tourism: A mixed-methods rhythmanalysis
authors: Wenjie Cai, Brad McKenna, 李善仕, Scott Cohen, Lena Waizenegger, René Riedl
summary: Tourism research has largely treated well-being as a motivation or outcome, neglecting how it unfolds in-situ and relying on self-report data. Through a mixed-methods rhythmanalysis, this study examines how well-being emerges and evolves in digital-free tourism. Following 23 participants through three-night digital-free cabin stays, we integrate electrodermal activity, interviews, and diaries to capture embodied experiences of disconnection. Participants experienced rhythmic re-attunement from linear, digital temporalities towards cyclical, embodied rhythms aligned with nature and interpersonal connection. Physiological data showed varied responses to disconnection and fewer detected skin conductance responses post-trip, supporting qualitative accounts of calm and rhythmic re-attunement. Through attunement, plenitude, stillness, and reflexivity, we reconceptualise well-being as a dynamic rhythmic process shaped through embodied experiences, environmental cues, and relational synchrony.

title: Global Genres, Local Shakespeare(s): Gender and Intertexulity in Post-Independence Tamil Films
summary: This dissertation examines the intertwined histories of Shakespeare and post-independence Tamil cinema through close readings of four films: L.V. Prasad's Manohara (1954), P. Neelakantan's Ambikapathi (1957), A.T. Krishnaswamy's Arivaali (1963), and Dada Mirasi's Rathathilagam (1963). Drawing on intertextuality, gender, and genre conventions as its primary methodological framework, this project argues that post-independence Tamil filmmakers engaged with Shakespeare not as a canonical authority but as one interlocutor among many in a multicultural, discursive history involving gender, justice, and cultural identity that long preceded him. By placing Shakespeare in dialogue with a wide range of Tamil and pan-Indian literary and performative traditions—including Valmiki's Ramayana, Kambar's Ramavataram, Ilanko Atikal's Silapadikaram, the Sangam poetic tradition, Thiruvalluvar's Kural, Subramania Bharathiyar's poetry of women's freedom and dignity, and Pammal Sambandha Mudaliar's pioneerin...

title: Con Proust entre las manos: la literatura latinoamericana a partir de sus porosidades proustianas
summary: This dissertation examines Latin American literary works produced since the 1940s across three distinct moments—modernity, mid-century, and contemporaneity—tracing their engagement with Marcel Proust’s novel À la recherche du temps perdu (1913–1927). The concept of “porosity,” inspired by María Zambrano, draws on the metaphor of the “porous body” that transforms the light that permeates it to articulate a philosophy of reading. Through a critical analysis of a literary corpus from diverse regions, this study reveals the persistent presence of Proust, whose work functions as a comparative reference for understanding those historical moments in which the subject—whether woman, writer, or artist—experiences the surrounding world. These readings intersect with gender studies, sensory studies, nostalgia, art, and world literature. The dissertation is structured around three case studies. title: Fictions of Filth: Race, Caste, and Empire in Late-Colonial India
summary: Fictions of Filth: Race, Caste, and Empire in Late-Colonial India, intervenes in the field of South Asian Studies through an analysis of literary representations of dirt, disease, and pollution in early-twentieth-century South Asia. I argue that the evolving terrain of filth was invested with multiple values during this period of high-imperialism, Hindu nationalism, and anti-caste activism in colonial India, making it a unique site for examining the reverberations of empire in the twenty-first century, especially in the context of the climate crisis. Literary representations of this period synthesize the socio-economic tensions into legible images and stories, thereby offering critical insights into under-examined imbrications and conflicts. I employ discourse analysis, in the school of Edward Said, and historicist literary criticism on the lines of Aijaz Ahmad, as my analytical tools for this interdisciplinary project. title: Literature After Performance: Contemporary Literature's Turn to Performance Art
summary: Literature After Performance is borne out of a series of observations regarding the attractions and antinomies between literature and performance in the contemporary era. Following the “turn to performance” in the late twentieth-century, this dissertation argues that while performance has emerged as an explanatory paradigm across numerous academic disciplines, literary studies has yet to engage meaningfully with performance theory and criticism—despite contemporary authors’ evident and increasing engagements with performance art in their literary works. Addressing the critical lacuna between performance studies and literary studies, Literature After Performance identifies a clear trend toward aesthetic performance within contemporary literature and, following the provocations of these texts, endeavors to bring the theoretical insights of performance studies to literary criticism. title: Collected: Trauma, Wonder, and the Birth of the Modern Museum Movement
summary: This dissertation investigates the life and collecting practices of Joseph Allen Skinner (1862–1946), a Holyoke, Massachusetts silk manufacturer, philanthropist, and childhood survivor of the Mill River Flood disaster of 1874, and the museum he created in South Hadley, Massachusetts, which he bequeathed to Mount Holyoke College upon his death. Drawing on material culture studies, the history of emotions, and scholarship in trauma and neuroscience, it argues that Skinner's lifelong collecting habits and eventual museum-making were shaped by two intertwined emotional responses to catastrophic loss: trauma and wonder. Chapter II, "Trauma Collected," examines Skinner's accumulation of Mill River flood relics—illustrated newspapers, silk remnants, a six-ton chunk of a broken dam—as material responses to disaster that persisted across seven decades. title: El lado más oscuro de la modernidad española: desindustrialización y narrativas culturales contrahegemónicas
summary: This doctoral dissertation analyzes deindustrialization in Spain as a structural process of the modern capitalist project and as the dark side of modernity, whose political, cultural, and ecological effects continue to shape landscapes, bodies, memories, and ways of life in the present. Against the hegemonic narratives of modernization, progress, and democratic consolidation articulated during the Transition, this study shifts attention toward industrial and postindustrial peripheries in order to examine experiences, subjects, and territories historically relegated to the margins of national memory. Drawing on an interdisciplinary approach that brings together cultural and film studies with theories of memory and ruins, as well as gender, queer, ecocritical, and decolonial perspectives, this dissertation examines a corpus of cultural productions, primarily contemporary documentary cinema, emerging from the context of deindustrialization in different territories of the Spanish state, wi...

title: Speak of the (She)Devil- Ontologies of Death and Female Life-Making Praxes in Folk-telling of The Bahamas
summary: In the 'unknown' moments between livingness and dying, or earth and heaven, myth or folklore are to be made or to be found. The recovery of folklore is not an unfamiliar project in the West Indian writing canon, but this manuscript is specified in its turn to the living expressive, spiritual, and religious culture of The Bahamas using the folkloric tradition. With written folklore, I ask for a reformation of the genre of the 'living word' or the 'sacred text,' for the folk tale, with its religious material or doctrine/s, meets the generic criteria. In religious formalism or theological 'orthodoxy,' the sacred text is culled by a high [‘heavenly’] power and/or an apostle [or clergy] trained in the practice, but that sacred material is curated also in the vernacular, by the commonfolk. The 'traditional' sacred text genre, it seems, is expressively delimited also, and 'non-traditional' or 'non-orthodox' religions of the West Indies, such as Obeah, can gain place in the formal medium of wr...

title: Deviant poetics: A new diction for the event of death through the vernaculars of the social-first moving image
summary: This practice-led thesis investigates the social-first moving image (Kaufman 2025; Vernallis 2023) as a necropolitical device (Preciado 2014; Mbembe 2003). Proliferating on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, and Google Maps, the banalisation of the event of death (Rankine 2004; Mroué 2006) through its circulation within the ordinary (Berlant 2006; Joseph 2021) produces a new form of sovereignty: holding power not over one’s mortality but over one’s ability for mourning (McCalden 2024; Rose 1995). Developed through a series of moving image works created between 2021 and 2025, this practice-led thesis identifies three distinct vernaculars through which the social-first moving image sets up a new way of speaking casually about death (Ibrahim 2021; Jurgenson 2019): the diaristic (user-generated daily chronicles), the recursive (algorithmic virality), and the navigational (interactive spatial renderings). title: Symbolic Translation: Psychoanalysis, Race, and the Korean/American Subject
summary: This dissertation introduces ‘symbolic translation’ as a new critical framework, developed through Lacanian psychoanalysis, to theorize Korean/American subjectivity as a condition of structural misrecognition, symbolic illegibility, and forced assimilation. I define symbolic translation as the reconfiguration of being in response to exclusion from the dominant Symbolic Order. Bridging Lacanian psychoanalytic theory with Asian American studies, the project interrogates how dominant Symbolic Orders fail to fully recognize racialized Korean/American subjects, rendering them illegible within existing regimes of meaning. Departing from prevailing paradigms of cultural hybridity or ‘model minority’ assimilation, symbolic translation foregrounds the structural violence, forced displacement, and enduring illegibility imposed by those dominant orders. This dissertation critiques assimilationist narratives that promise seamless integration, revealing how such scripts mask ongoing structures of e...

title: "NOT WITH[OUT] MY HIJAB": A DIALOGIC PERFORMANCE ETHNOGRAPHY OF CRITICAL PEDAGOGY IN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
summary: Bakhtinian dialogism begins from a crowded scene: every utterance arrives already inhabited. This inquiry gathers around two Muslim women who enter the same educational space asymmetrically positioned and differently marked by hijab and by the racialized and political worlds that read it. Each arrives already answerable to those worlds. As their bodies are legislated, interpreted, rescued, and contained in public discourse, this dissertation traces how that weight enters language teaching and learning. Grounded in Diversi and Moreira's betweener and written as dialogic performance ethnography, this inquiry sustains two consciousnesses in answerable relation across eleven months of recorded collaboration between an Egyptian American educator-researcher and an Afghan refugee learner. title: Perth Girl on Mars
summary: Perth Girl on Mars is a creative dissemination of doctoral research exploring how the interior design of future Mars habitats can contribute to psychological wellbeing. Grounded in a two-week residency at the Mars Desert Research Station (MDRS) in the Utah Desert, the installation draws upon the researcher's reflective observations alongside interview and questionnaire responses from analogue astronauts who have inhabited the same space. This work focuses specifically on the sleeping quarters, or 'staterooms', positioning this intimate interior as the object under examination. More than a place to sleep, the room becomes a space of retreat, routine, identity, and emotional regulation, revealing how the built environment actively shapes human experience within isolated, confined, and extreme conditions. title: Presence / Absence
summary: Presence / Absence invites viewers to reconsider the concepts of ‘presence’ and ‘absence’ in contemporary life. Drawing on Merleau-Ponty’s phenomenology of perception—where presence is understood not simply as physical proximity but as an embodied experience of “being-in-the-world”—the installation examines how lived experience is shaped by what we attend to and asks us to consider what is relegated to the periphery. It is comprised of three ‘rooms’, each offering a dual interpretation of presence and absence: the Mediation Room, Meditation Room, and Naturation Room. Rather than presenting a fixed narrative, the installation asks visitors to determine how long they remain in each room, what they attend to, and how their own interpretations shape the work’s meaning. In doing so, it moves the concepts of presence and absence beyond a literal or binary framework and positions visitors as active participants, interpreter, and co-creators of aesthetic experiences. title: Making Ceramics for Sensory Public Architecture
summary: Exposed on the edge of ovals, sports pavilions operate as civic beacons—both as spaces of gathering, health, and community identity, but also inviting graffiti and vandalism. Funded by the community, these buildings should return value, not only through durability, but through the quality of sensory and emotional experience they provide. An overemphasis on durability, cost-efficiency, and risk mitigation too often produces buildings governed by a narrow, engineering-led logic—repetitive, austere, and emotionally disengaged. The research investigates how ceramic architectural elements might transform these often utilitarian environments through materiality, texture and tactile engagement. Positioning architecture as capable of eliciting positive emotional responses through sensory experience, it explores the latent potential of architectural surfaces to engage the body. title: Emplaced: A Sensory Tool for Exploring Place Attachment
summary: Our attachment to places is mediated through body - from the gritty feel of beach sand shifting underfoot, to the cool smooth turn of a brass doorknob underhand, to the papery rustle and distinctive smell of dry grass. Place attachment, the emotional bond between people and places, is shaped not only by social ties, memory and thought, but by embodied, sensory, experience (Scannell and Gifford 2010; Lewicka 2011; Degnen 2016). This project asks whether embodied interactions with objects can draw that bond to the surface, contributing to a better understanding of place attachment. Building on previous research utilising sensory autoethnography to explore connections between people and the non-human nature (Scherini 2022), the project pilots a community engagement tool that uses embodied interactions with objects to better understand place attachment. title: Geological Skin 111C
summary: This practice-led research investigates embodied responses to AI-generated portraits through hand-finished printmaking to address questions about how we recognise humanness when indexical relationships between image and subject dissolve. As AI-generated faces become indistinguishable from photographs, this work explores whether viewers can experience genuine emotional connection, what Roland Barthes termed the punctum, to synthetic faces that have never existed. The work engages a hybrid methodology: AI-generated portraits are transformed through traditional photo-etching, creating a three-dimensional tactile surface that contradicts the flatness of screens where such images typically exist. This process reveals a paradox: as surface-level indexical links decrease through digital synthesis, a "deeper likeness" emerges, not to any one person, but to our embodied understanding of humanness itself. title: Out of Hand
summary: Out of Hand is an interactive arcade installation that combines digital interaction design, computer vision, generative AI and object-based practice to examine how people read emotion, intention and even performative consciousness into a responsive machine. The installation repositions a familiar arcade cabinet as a personified encounter with Tomoko, an anime-styled Japanese high-school student who appears trapped inside a repeating game of rock paper scissors. Hand gestures replace buttons, not as a more efficient input method but as an ambiguous, situated form of communication: how a player moves across the three rounds shapes Tomoko's responses, and with them the player's own sympathy, attachment, discomfort or indifference toward her. The game's emotional trajectory is a deliberate subversion of traditional visual-novel conventions. title: Corporeal Cloth
summary: Corporeal Cloth is a practice-based research project that investigates clothing as an active archive of lived experience. Through continual engagement with the body, garments collect traces of wear, information about their lives as personal objects. Sitting between fashion and textile design, Corporeal Cloth employs interdisciplinary techniques to generate new knowledge about wear, value, reuse and object agency within contemporary design practice. The research is conducted through material experimentation, transforming post-consumer textile waste into a contemporary tailored trench coat. Iterative processes of layering, piecing, dyeing, stitching and pattern making function simultaneously as design methods and analytical tools. Through this approach, wear is reframed from a marker of obsolescence into an index of interaction, with the lived experience of cloth central to the design process. title: Wonderful Nothing
summary: Wonderful Nothing is a digital fashion project that questions how the fashion and textiles industry can continue to exist within socio-ecological boundaries to speculate whether a fashion and textiles industry that “withdraws” from its most obvious manifestation (clothing) might be reimagined amidst transformation and cultural belonging, where fashion without physical garments could be reframed as a creative ecosystem that focuses on style, identity and self-expression. Presented on a screen, Wonderful Nothing centres on a digital human form developed as a 3D object, formatted to store shape, colour, and texture data. Created using visualisation software vizcom, CLO3d and Adobe Photoshop, this ‘human-object’ is wrapped in a knitted, textured material to signify a digital boundary surface, where skin and cloth determine the inside from outside to reimagine the body's own surface as the site of design. title: Lozenging
summary: Lozenging is a material and spatial installation that explores the relationship between the cellular structure of cork oak, window frame and interior landscape grafting. Drawing on Robert Hooke’s Micrographia, where cork is first defined as a “cell” used in architecture, and Thomas Browne’s Quincuncial Lozenge, the installation moves one’s emotional lightness of being through the complexities of cork bark. Derived from everyday traffic scenes across construction sites, the “freeze-frame” stages the act of looking through and exchange. Lozenge-shaped apertures and Frank Lloyd Wright’s projected “corner window frame as innovation” foreground overlooked spatial conditions, transforming the gap between cork core and handmade frame into a static interface for experimentation. The installation’s grafted-cork framework, making process and collaborative logic draw on the Quincuncial Lozenge, understood as both a geometrical and spiritual network for arranging the pattern for planted trees. authors: Qassim Mohammed Saleh Saad, Tanja Glusac
summary: The Rhythm of the Ordinary Qassim Saad & Tanja Glusac This work explores repetition as a creative and critical concept, examined through phenomenological and embodied approaches. Responding to the CPRS 2026 context, the project treats the object as an active, affective entity, investigating how repeated slots, filled with objects drawn from nearby environments, domestic spaces, studios and workshops, generate embodied knowledge and sensory significance. Drawing on Merleau-Ponty's account of habit and motor intentionality (2012), repetition is positioned as a mode of atonement, a way of sensing the world through practice, rhythm and material engagement. In Husserl's account of lived experience (Erlebnis), repetition structures perception, with meaning emerging through temporal accumulation. title: Italian Journey
summary: In 1786, when he was already the acknowledged leader of the Sturm und Drang literary movement, Goethe set out on a journey to Italy to fulfil a personal and artistic quest and to find relief from his responsibilities and the agonies of unrequited love. As he travelled to Venice, Rome, Naples and Sicily he wrote many letters, which he later used as the basis for the Italian Journey. A journal full of fascinating observations on art and history, and the plants, landscape and the character of the local people he encountered, this is also a moving account of the psychological crisis from which Goethe emerged newly inspired to write the great works of his mature years.

title: Answerability: Exhibition, Documentation, and Historical Evidence in Postwar Japanese Art
summary: This working paper develops a claim-specific criterion of historical answerability through engagement with Reiko Tomii’s scholarship on operation in postwar Japanese art. It asks when evidence concerning exhibition, documentation, and artistic organization requires an art-historical account to reconsider the boundary of the work it claims to explain.The principal case is Shiraga Kazuo’s Challenging Mud. Tomii’s accounts of material preparation and anticipated display are read beside Namiko Kunimoto’s analysis of action, object, agency, and selfhood. Further investigations address press presentation and photographic selection, Hi Red Center and GUN, conditions of authorization, and the differentiation of events and photographic records in museum cataloguing. The comparison does not presume a disagreement between Tomii and Kunimoto or equate evidence of preparation with complete predetermination.The method distinguishes attribution, justification, and historical accuracy. title: Medieval Arabic Dance: Philosophical and Speculative Foundations of the Performing Arts in the Abbasid Era
summary: This paper reconstructs, through a textual and philosophical reading of selected Abbasid-era sources, the pre-expressive foundations of medieval Arabic court dance as an integrated performing art rather than a recoverable “catalogue of steps.” Methodologically, it advances an interpretive hypothesis grounded primarily in al-Fārābī's Kitāb al-mūsīqī al-kabīr and al-Masʿūdī's Murūj al-Ḏahab, supplemented by reflections drawn from al-Kindī's musical theory, while delimiting the investigation to the Abbasid period (second half of the 8th to the first half of the 13th century). The author is a performing scholar—dancer, choreographer, and researcher—whose analysis emerges from nearly thirty years of embodied practice in Arab-Islamic and Persian dance forms, and whose dancer-philosopher perspective combines firsthand performance experience with rigorous philological inquiry. title: Visual metaphors of liminality in Edward Hopper's paintings
authors: Oleksandr Yudenko, Наталія Кравченко, Tetiana Davydova, Nelia Zuienko
summary: This study examines liminality in Edward Hopper’s paintings through the analytical lens of visual metaphor, foregrounding how pictorial elements construct threshold experience. Liminality, understood as a state ‘betwixt and between,’ entails suspended temporality, spatial indeterminacy, and destabilized existential boundaries. While Hopper’s work has been widely discussed within art history, the metaphorical structures through which liminality is visually constructed have not been previously theorized. The article demonstrates that Hopper’s environments function as metaphorical projections of psychological and ontological states. Solitary houses operate as visual metaphors of the human condition: anthropomorphized facades stand for isolation, sealed or darkened windows for emotional opacity, and architectural stillness for temporal arrest. title: Design beyond borders: Negotiating connection and identity across nations
summary: Design in the twenty-first century embodies a productive paradox: it is at once a force that connects cultures through global circulation and a medium for expressing cultural and national identities. It evolves relentlessly — every day, every hour — often outpacing our ability to record or preserve its recent past. What was groundbreaking yesterday may already feel distant today, as design moves forward with remarkable speed, disregarding boundaries of nation, style, or tradition. The digital age, with its unprecedented access to ideas and methods, allows nearly anyone to follow emerging trends in real time. Yet this openness also highlights the importance of context: the way design is applied, understood, or valued continues to vary across different cultural and intellectual landscapes. This article explores design as a “boundary practice”: a field that creates shared languages across borders while also safeguarding diversity by preserving cultural differences. summary: Direct interaction between the stage and the audience in European theater, from Antiquity to the present day, is a subject as vast as the cultural, geographical, and temporal scope of the phenomenon. This paper proposes an analysis of the two fundamental types of interaction with the audience—direct and indirect—in the early days of theater. summary: The ongoing intersection of science and the humanities reflects a broader movement known as “H-STEM,” which integrates humanistic inquiry with science, technology, engineering, and mathematics to foster more holistic approaches to scientific discovery and innovation. title: The Visibility Paradox : Expertise, Authority, and the Attention Economy in the Digital Age
summary: This monograph investigates a paradox that has become emblematic of the contemporary public sphere: individuals and institutions with the deepest epistemic qualifications—decades of formal training, peer-reviewed publications, and accumulated professional experience—systematically command the least public attention, while individuals with minimal qualifications command the most. title: Historical distance: affective practice in immersive heritage at the Mogao Caves, China
summary: Heritage institutions increasingly invest in immersive experiences, yet research often treats affect as a consequence of immersion rather than a force that shapes how visitors relate to the past. In the context of conservation at the Mogao Caves, this study examines how three immersive settings—regulated visits to the original caves, replica exhibitions, and the E-Dunhuang virtual tour—organise historical distance and how visitors negotiate it through affective practice. Drawing on participant observation and interviews with 22 Chinese domestic visitors, it shows that regulated access at the original site produces a concentrated encounter; open-ended viewing and spatial constraints in replicas invite negotiation between proximity and distance; and repeatable, interface-driven navigation in the virtual tour enables visitors to develop personal connections gradually. summary: Tanqīd or Urdu literary criticism developed along with the changing socio-political landscape. At the same time, we need to acknowledge the agency of literary critics in engaging with the historical challenges in which they were couched. Understanding the literary cultures of Tanqīd hence requires addressing Urdu literary criticism as a historically situated practice, exploring how literary critics have engaged with literature in different modes of temporality. The classical period of Urdu literature, which impressed upon the language mastery of the poet to weave intricate verses, is best captured in Mir Taqi Mir’s Nikāt ush-Shu’arā (1752). With complete colonial domination, 1857 marked a watershed, which forced an inward critique on the part of the Urdu intelligentsia. title: Values of Villainy: A Typology of Antagonists in Superhero Films Through Schwartz’s Theory of Basic Human Values
summary: This article investigates the motivational grammars of villains in Hollywood superhero films through the lens of Schwartz’s Theory of Basic Human Values. By analyzing the discourse of eight iconic antagonists, we identified three clusters: Ambiguous Tragedians, whose villainy emerges from wounded subjectivity and marginalization; Revolutionary Calculators, who justify domination through distorted appeals to justice and order; and the Chaotic Nihilist, represented solely by Heath Ledger’s Joker, who embodies systemic collapse and anarchic spectacle. The findings show that villains operate as moral rhetoricians, dramatizing value tensions, distortions, and voids. These insights highlight the potential of integrating psychological theory and film analysis, while also pointing to new agendas for cross-cultural, multimodal, and reception-oriented studies of villainy.

Trata-se de uma pesquisa qualitativa, de caráter descritivo e exploratório, desenvolvida por meio de análise documental da Base Nacional Comum Curricular (BNCC), do Documento de Referência Curricular de Mato Grosso (DRC-MT) e de Projetos Político-Pedagógicos (PPPs) escolares. Os resultados indicam que a BNCC apresenta uma abordagem generalista da EA, sem direcionamentos metodológicos específicos para o uso do teatro. O DRC-MT, por sua vez, amplia as possibilidades ao propor articulações interdisciplinares e metodologias ativas, favorecendo a integração entre teatro e EA. Já os PPPs analisados evidenciam a presença incipiente do teatro e sua desvinculação das práticas de EA. title: Pliny's Varro: Source, Inspiration, Competition
summary: The shadow of M. Terentius Varro, Rome’s great Republican polymath, looms long over the preface to Pliny’s Naturalis historia, a strangely Menippean blend of epistolary prose, Catullan allusions, quotidian slang, and Greekified learning. Pliny freely employs emblematic Varronian verbs to describe his scholarly labour, but offers a recusatio against following the models of Varro’s own Disciplinae and Antiquitates. By colonising the neutral ground of res naturae and adopting the paradoxical format of the ordered miscellany, Pliny positions his Imperial project as a carefully crafted counterpoint to the stupendous challenge that Varro’s works posed to posterity. Pliny’s agonistic ambivalence towards Varro, his chief source, chief inspiration, but also chief competition, can be further investigated by examining the awkward and kaleidoscopic image of Varro that lies latent in the body of the Naturalis historia.

title: Happy Anniversary
summary: This chapter introduces readers to John Herbers. A white southerner, Herbers built his career writing for Mississippi newspapers, and for the United Press (later UPI). Along the way, he often found himself writing stories about racial turmoil, such as his coverage of the murder trial of Emmett Till. In the summer of 1963, Herbers is hired by The New York Times to join the race beat. It is a breakthrough for his career, but it sets him up for an extremely stressful year in his family with his wife and four young daughters. He will constantly be on the go. In mid-September, he is due back home in Atlanta to see his family for the first time in weeks, but on the way to the airport, he hears about the bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church. He turns the car around and plunges into a most challenging reporting situation. Among other things, he winds up interviewing the parents of the four girls who were killed in the bombing. He also misses his anniversary at home.

title: School Bells Ringing

Labor Day weekend in St. Augustine includes some protests at the Plaza. Police use dogs and cattle prods, and a number of people are arrested, including Robert Hayling. The school year begins on Tuesday. At still-segregated Murray High School, the absence of the St. Augustine Four (Audrey Nell Edwards, JoeAnn Anderson, Willie Carl Singleton, and Samuel White) is conspicuous. At the Fullerwood Elementary School, fourth grader Irwin Brunson has his first day and begins to sense the difficulty of the journey ahead.

title: The Play Is the Thing
summary: This chapter, the first of Part 5, explores the world Martin Luther King is facing by early March, 1964. His treasured philosophy of nonviolence is teetering. The Civil Rights Bill is facing a near-certain filibuster in the Senate. There are all manner of internal stresses, ranging from his own frenetic schedule, to increasing FBI scrutiny, to a turbulent personal life. King realizes that he needs one more stage to dramatize racial injustice as the Civil Rights Bill is up for grabs. His staff makes several cases of places that would be suitable for direct action. One of those, pushed by Hosea Williams, is St. Augustine. Meanwhile, Robert Hayling has begun reaching out to civil rights leaders in search of an organization to back his efforts for equality in the city. On March 6, when King and his SCLC staff are expected at a meeting in Orlando, Hayling drives out to meet them.

title: True Conditions
summary: The first chapter of Part 6, this one begins by focusing on St. Augustine Mayor Joseph Shelley, a staunch defender of the city’s reputation. A self-described segregationist, Shelley believes that the city did not have any racial problems until “outside agitators came in.” He is particularly angered by Mary Peabody’s claims of racism on the NBC Today show. He pushes hard for equal time, and gets the network to agree. Shelley then travels up to Washington D.C. for the filming with an entourage that includes Sheriff L.O. Davis. Shelley’s efforts to defend the city’s honor warrant four straight days of Page 1 stories in the St. Augustine Record. At the same time, the second wave of SCLC activism begins in the city. summary: A pair of short stories from Parallax · Twin Tales, which stage one real dilemma twice: Here, in the world as it is, with invented people in real rooms; There, in the world of Vision Come True, a future that split from ours in 2024 and never emerged. Here, in Geneva, a fact-checker finds that her newspaper's most trusted reporter is right about almost everything, and that the newsroom's AI checker confirmed him by counting copies of his own story; she prints what could not be established. There, in Rhône's Elbow in 2035, two communes ask an intelligence to certify or to cast doubt on a grazing right of 1593; she sends a swarm of scouts, finds the one line the record is silent about, and tells both sides how far they may disagree.
