title: Epilogue: What Must Be Remembered
summary: The epilogue covers the next sixty years, from July 1964 through July 2024. Readers see the many changes in St. Augustine and its continued struggles to grapple with racial tension. Many areas of progress are noted, particularly the attempts by a group called ACCORD to preserve the history of civil rights in the city. There has also been backlash, many tense struggles over how to handle the past, including a fierce battle over what to do with the Confederate Memorial in the Plaza. The chapter explores the trajectory of many of the people who were part of that drama in the 1960s. Many have died. Some old-timers remain. Black neighborhoods have become significantly gentrified. The book concludes with an account of a banquet on July 2, 2024, to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the signing of the Civil Rights Act. One of the keynote speakers is Crystal Hayling, youngest daughter of the late dentist who spearheaded the movement for change.

title: The Problem We All Live With
summary: Set on January 14, 1964, this chapter focuses primarily on Norman Rockwell, the painter long known for a glorified nostalgia about America. Nearing his 70th birthday, Rockwell has tired of the pressure from the Saturday Evening Post to aggrandize the country and to ignore issues like racial tension. He makes a break from the magazine that had made him famous for 47 years. On this day in 1964, he shocks many of his fans with a painting in Look magazine called “The Problem We All Live With.” The painting depicts 6-year-old Ruby Bridges, a Black girl in a white dress striding into school in New Orleans accompanied by federal marshals. The painting takes place against a backdrop of racism: the painted word “N*****,” the letters “KKK,” and a blood-like splat of tomato. On the same day in Florida, the St. Augustine Four are finally set free and returned home.

title: Black Snow
summary: This chapter, the first of Part 3, introduces readers to Stetson Kennedy, a maverick white southerner with a passion for racial justice and a willingness to explore unconventional means to achieve it. Born in Jacksonville, Florida, Kennedy became a folklorist who worked with Zora Neale Hurston on the Federal Writers Project. He ultimately wrote some provocative books, including Jim Crow Guide to the USA and I Rode With the Klan (later retitled The Klan Unmasked). After many years as an expatriate, Kennedy returned to Florida in the early sixties and began writing about civil rights for the Pittsburgh Courier, a renowned African-American newspaper. Writing under the pseudonym Snow James, Kennedy provided a vivid account of the Klan rally after interviewing Robert Hayling, whose first-person perspectives were notably ignored by the hometown St. Augustine Record.

summary: The introduction explores the author’s path into writing this book. The introduction spells out the book’s focus and structure. It examines St. Augustine, Florida, the oldest city in the United States, one with a fascinating racial history that speaks volumes about the country’s history and present-day struggles. The stress deepens when he is contacted by a local Black minister asking Irv to “do a little spy work” at a scheduled Ku Klux Klan rally just outside of St. Augustine. title: Light Going Out
summary: Set on November 22, 1963, this chapter explores the experience of some of the book’s characters on the day when President Kennedy is assassinated. title: Before the Photocell, the Eye An essay on a painting by Lavinia Falcan
summary: The first thing one notices in Lavinia Falcan’s painting is the eyes. They are large, wide open, outlined in black against fields of cobalt, turquoise and violet, and almost none of them look at the viewer. They look past us, sideways, upward, towards something outside the frame. The faces around them are fragmented and recombined in the manner of the early twentieth century, but the eyes stay whole. Everything else in the picture may dissolve into colour; the act of looking does not. This is a fitting image for the scientists the painting calls to mind. Long before physics had instruments to measure light, it had the eye, and for most of history the eye was the instrument

title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps When We're Cold or Scared?
summary: Have you ever noticed tiny bumps rise on your arms during a cold morning, or felt the same prickle during a scary scene in amovie? That reaction is called goosebumps, and in this article I explain the biology behind it. You will learn about a tinymuscle attached to every hair on your body, why the exact same reflex fires whether you are freezing or frightened, and whythis “leftover” reaction from our furrier ancestors still switches on today even though it barely helps modern humansanymore. By the end, you will understand why a chilly breeze and a moving song can make your skin do exactly the samething.

authors: 1*Dr. Vishali Mankotia, 2Dr. R.M.S. Kushwah, 3Dr. Pooja Makhnotra, 4Dr. Pooja Thakur
summary: Ayurveda, the foundational Indian science of medicine, offers a highly sophisticated framework for understanding human anatomy and physiology. Classical authorities like Acharya Charaka and Acharya Sushruta documented the skin (Twacha) extensively, defining it in the Sushruta Samhita as the primary anatomical seat of tactile perception (Adhishthana of Sparshanendriya). Far from being a passive external envelope, Twacha is recognized as a dynamic structure intricately linked to tissue nourishment (Dhatu Poshana), systemic equilibrium, and metabolic vitality. Similarly, contemporary biomedical science identifies the skin as the largest organ of the integumentary system, acting as a crucial immunological barrier and sensory interface. While most cutaneous disorders carry low mortality rates, their profound impact on psychological well-being and life quality underscores the clinical value of precise anatomical insights.

title: Memory and Emergence
summary: A negative contains all the information for the final photographic print. But held up against the light, the negative often appears glaring and garish—certainly unfamiliar and sometimes difficult to recognize. Immediately after exposure in the quiet acrid environment of the darkroom, the positive enlargement is initially invisible and then starts to appear so faintly that it is scarcely detectable; only with patience as it reacts to the harsh chemical baths into which it was plunged does it emerge into a sharp, detailed, and nuanced image. In the shadows cast by the negative, as the resultant positive emerges from the nearly unrecognizable past, it is surprising and gratifying to discover a memory of the initial moment of exposure. This metaphor serves as an apt though abstract description of the experiences described in this essay.

title: A Theology of Temporal Placement: An Archival Hermeneutic for the Management and Preservation of Unanswerable Trauma
summary: Contemporary philosophical theology and pastoral trauma discourses frequently operate under a rigid imperative of immediate therapeutic resolution, forced emotional integration, or premature ethical reconciliation. When confronting severe, transgenerational existential ruptures—events that are historically unverifiable, relationally non-reciprocal, or permanently unresolved—this demand for immediate closure constitutes a form of secondary institutional violence. This paper introduces A Theology of Temporal Placement (Temporal Placement Hermeneutics). Shifting the fundamental theological locus from "How to solve or eliminate suffering?" to "How to order, defer, and entrust the unfinished within the divine architecture?", this methodology deploys the Apothecary Cabinet not as a passive psychological defense, but as a rigorous, four-tier archival system for human survival, preservation, and ultimate redemptive testimony.

title: Conspiracy care work: gender, labor, and the paranoid style in American podcasting (2012-2020)
summary: There is a dominant conception, both in academic literature and most media, that conspiracy theorists are mostly men—think “toxic masculinity” in internet culture. Apple’s built-in podcast app and the success of true crime podcast Serial (2014) heralded an era of prestige audio with conspiracy as a central theme and women as their paranoid protagonists. summary: Folk art is constantly changing. title: THE SEMIOTIC BREACH
authors: Dr Pushpendra Kumar, Chaudhary Mayank, Raj prince, Raj Kritika, Jatavath sriram
summary: For decades, the discourse surrounding drug-resistant pathogens has been imprisoned within the crude vocabulary of warfare. We speak endlessly of miracle drugs, frontline defenses, last-resort armaments, and pathogenic enemies laying siege to human health. This militaristic conceit is not merely a poetic flourish; it is a fundamental cognitive error that obscures the biological reality of microbial systems. Bacteria are not hostile combatants invading an alien territory; they are the baseline architects of Earth's biogeochemical machinery. When we introduce concentrated synthetic molecules to eliminate them, we are not waging war—we are writing software updates for a planetary biological network that reads chemical interventions as raw data.

title: Introduction
summary: Abstract The Introduction lays out the book’s guiding distinction between sense—what speakers do in making themselves intelligible—and meaning, the truth-conditional content of what they say. A statement can lack sense without lacking meaning, as Moore’s Paradox (“p, but I don't believe that p”) shows; variants recurring across belief, action, desire, exhortation, aesthetic judgment, and validity form the book’s central diagnostic. Two theses, pursued in every chapter, are introduced: that an attitude is constituted in part by our special way of knowing we hold it (Shoemaker) and that the standards to which it is answerable partly constitute what it is (Hieronymi). These converge in the thinker’s capacity to avow her attitudes, whose exercise just is an application of the relevant standard. Against Gricean, inferentialist pictures of uptake, understanding what someone says is not an inference to her state of mind but a grasp of the sense she makes.

title: Bodies in Motion: Images of Women in the Magazine Frou-Frou (Rio de Janeiro, 1923–1927)
summary: In the 1920s, Rio de Janeiro emerged as a cosmopolitan capital marked by rapid urban development and profound social change. During this period, women experienced greater freedom of movement and expanded opportunities for participation in social life outside the home. At the same time, fashion underwent radical change: while Paris remained an important reference point, North American influences—circulating primarily through cinema—gained increasing prominence. These shifts generated a growing demand for information, which people hoped to find above all in the numerous illustrated magazines then in circulation. One such magazine was Frou-Frou, which sought to provide elite women with advice on the challenges of modern city life. In response to new beauty ideals, the magazine focused on the representations of the female body. This article analyzes the roles of beach life and sports in this context and the extent to which these two topics attracted readers’ interest.

title: The Unitarians

This insightful work examines Unitarianism’s intellectual shifts, its emphasis on freedom in religion, and its enduring faith, making it essential for understanding this progressive tradition. This book will be of interest to students of religion.

title: Recognition as Blessing in Post-Resurrection Drama and The Winter's Tale
summary: Medieval resurrection plays—dramatizing Mary Magdalene at the tomb, the disciples on the Emmaus road, and Doubting Thomas—offer Shakespeare a rich theatrical model for recognition as blessing. In these plays, misrecognition is not a failure to be corrected but a necessary stage of faith, where doubt and inner longing prepare characters to receive what they cannot yet see. This chapter traces that tradition from Catholic and Protestant Communion practice through the resurrection drama of York, Chester, and elsewhere, arguing that Shakespeare inherits from it a vision of recognition as gift rather than achievement—one that shapes the final scene of The Winter&s;s Tale , where Leontes receives Hermione not through earning her but through disavowing any claim to moral reckoning and simply being open to the experience.

title: Toxic Dissonances

summary: This chapter explores Raymond’s descriptions of military engagements and demonstrates that they are shaped by biblical and symbolic patterns rather than by purely tactical concerns. The study shows that Raymond adapts the topos of heavenly intervention while reframing it within a scriptural matrix distinct from the Gesta Francorum tradition. Numerical exaggeration, recurring symbolic figures, and portrayals of overwhelming enemy forces serve to heighten the providential dimension of conflict. The chapter concludes that Raymond’s military narratives should be read as theological historiography, in which victory confirms divine favour and reinforces communal identity.

title: Introduction
summary: Recognition shapes the history of moral philosophy as much as it shapes dramatic narrative—and these two traditions have more to do with one another than is commonly assumed. This introduction traces recognition from classical anagnorisis through Hobbes, Hegel, and Levinas. It argues that the history of moral philosophy is itself a history of “primal scenes”: imagined encounters between two parties in competition for life, freedom, or identity. Shakespeare&s;s plays engage these primal scenes not deductively but heuristically, staging recognition as a festive, chance-driven event that suspends tragic inevitability. Drawing on medieval devotion and Ricoeur&s;s notion of festive recognition, the introduction argues that Shakespearean anagnorisis transacts reconciliation not through moral reckoning but through symbolic exchange.

title: A political-ontological perspective on pluriversal time
summary: This article outlines a framework for understanding the relation between pluriversality and the temporalities of just transitions. We draw on political ontology, a field that examines conflicts between the modern ontology – grounded in the separation of humans from nature – and other ways of understanding and inhabiting the world that conceive of the planet as a living whole and humans as integral to an intelligent cosmos and the living Earth. The metaphor helps us convey both the consequences of modern monoversal worldmaking and the potential of pluriversal struggles to challenge dominant narratives and assumptions about reality. title: The cultural evolution of play and magic dolls across 110 societies
summary: Dolls represent one of the most widespread and enduring material objects that humans create across societies. The pervasiveness of dolls can offer novel insights into the role of human material culture in processes of cultural evolution. While commonly considered children's toys and discussed in relation to childhood play, in many societies dolls are also employed for magical purposes. Here, we examine the dual use of dolls to inform us about the cultural evolution of supernatural beliefs and magic. We made use of the electronic Human Relations Area Files (eHRAF) to identify different types of dolls and their uses across societies in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample (SCCS). Across 110 societies, two distinct doll types emerged, some for play, and others for magic. Furthermore, dolls are used in magic practices 1) as tools to punish adversaries, 2) for protection or healing, 3) to increase fertility, and 4) to embody spirits. title: My late grandmother
summary: Conceptual work exploring memory, loss, and the inevitability of delay ("you are born to be late!"). Created using recycled paper, soil, and saliva. Version I was accidentally destroyed, turning this piece into a second-edition recreation that physically embodies the imperfection of human memory and bodily decay. The portrait reflects on the nature of old age: a profound regression into the biological and the defiled (soil, saliva) — the very essence of childhood. In old age, we turn back into children: biologically defenseless beings, constantly stained as we navigate existence. Old age is thus revealed as a second childhood, which, like the first, possesses its own absolute conclusion: death.

title: Violin duets in instrumental teaching, performance and music-making in the UK
summary: Abstract The violin duet has long occupied a relevant place within instrumental pedagogy, forming part of the canon of the major historic violin schools and included in recent syllabi of some music performance graded examinations. Scholarship has identified numerous pedagogical benefits from duets. This qualitative interview study explores 31 UK teachers’ perceptions of the types of duetting activity within their violin teaching and the factors influencing their inclusion of duets. These have implications for the ongoing use of duets due to their potentially limited performance visibility, associations with amateurism and contextual aspects such as provision of pianos in teaching spaces, which warrant consideration in relation to the future development of the genre.

title: From the Bazaar to the Algorithm: AI as a Technology Friend, Not a Human Friend
summary: This paper explores the philosophical and architectural implications of artificial intelligence, arguing that AI should be understood as a historical continuation of tools rather than an independent agent. Focusing on the core concept of the "technology friend," the study examines the dangers of profit-driven design choices that simulate human relationships, foster emotional dependency, and obscure responsibility. It proposes alternative frameworks, such as structural boundaries, non-deceptive interface design, and bridging mechanisms to human communities, offering a perspective at the intersection of the philosophy of technology, AI ethics, and cognitive science.

title: Symbiosis on Acid
summary: This article examines the relationship between Gaian ecology and psychedelic experience in the fiction of Ursula K. Le Guin and the work of ethnobotanist and psychonaut Terence McKenna. Both authors use psychedelics to open perspectives on symbiosis as a model for more equitable human–nature relationships, Le Guin through the association of planetary symbiosis with a cooperative alien society and McKenna via the figure of Gaia as ‘planetary Other’ with the capacity to dissolve ‘steep walls of cultural inflexibility’. Yet they differ in how they position psychedelics as delivering access to these visions of symbiotic partnership. Comparing Le Guin’s and McKenna’s visions of psychedelic ecology reveals some of the tensions that tie psychedelics to visions of ecological systems, humanism, and technology in the late twentieth century—and the association of psychedelics as such with both post- and ultra-human futures.

title: Fast Astronomical Transients in Archival Photographic Plates: Using optical aberrations as a tool for discerning real images, from plate artifacts
summary: The detection of fast astronomical transients in photographic plates from the Palomar sky surveys conducted in the 1950s, was subject to the criticism that such transients could be just the effect of otherwise unaccounted for plate artifacts. In this paper, we show that transient images exhibit the coma aberration pattern expected from off-axis point sources recorded through the telescope optics, a signature that plate artifacts cannot naturally reproduce. Although the data does not by themselves establish the physical origin of the light that generated the images, they lend support to hypotheses that do not rely on instrumental effects to explain transients.

This study aims to identify and describe the symbolic meanings embodied in the Wete Wu’u customary tradition among the community of Riangkotek Village, Lewolema District, East Flores Regency. A descriptive qualitative design was employed, grounded in the triadic semiotic framework of Charles Sanders Peirce. Data were collected through field observations, in-depth interviews with customary elders (ata klake), and documentary studies of ritual artifacts. The findings reveal that ritual paraphernalia operates as an integrated sign system linking representamen, objects, and interpretants. E...

title: Exploraciones digestivas. La relación estética y conceptual entre cine y performance en la película Crímenes del futuro de David Cronenberg
summary: The paper argues that the film Crimes of the Future opens up a critical dialogue on the relationship between the body and technology through two controversial figures in the world of performance art: Orlan and Stelarc. The tensions arising from this relationship are framed by the premise that the evolution of bodies is not to be found in the body-machine hybridisation and prosthetics; rather, it lies in the mysterious rebellion of the organs: the organ in question—or rather, the system in conflict—is here the digestive system. Digestion is therefore explored as the film’s acoustic identity, as an aesthetic experience, and as the conceptual framework for the analytical writing of this text.

title: Die Panne by Friedrich Dürrenmatt: A Trial for the Concept of Justice
summary: This essay critically examines Friedrich Dürrenmatt’s Die Panne as a profound metaphor for the complexities and perversions of justice in modern society. Dürrenmatt constructs a narrative that subverts traditional detective story conventions, presenting a reverse trial in which the protagonist, Alfredo Traps, is led to accept responsibility for a death that cannot be established as murder in legal terms. Through a mock trial staged by retired legal professionals, the story explores justice, morality, and the human condition, revealing the grotesque consequences that arise when an aesthetically compelling judgment takes the place of evidentiary certainty. The essay examines Dürrenmatt’s critique of both public justice (Justiz) and moral justice (Gerechtigkeit), while emphasizing the unresolved relation between Traps’s legal innocence, his ethical responsibility, and the narrative construction of guilt. Reading the prose narrative in relation to its framework and, where relevant, to the ...

title: Eisenstein y la calavera: ¿una Danza macabra modernizada o la construcción de un símbolo?
summary: This article analyzes the construction of the skull and the Day of the Dead as national symbols in the Epilogue of Sergei Eisenstein's film project, ¡Que Viva México! (1930–32). In particular, the Epilogue episode—dedicated to José Guadalupe Posada and the Day of the Dead—represents a modern, post-revolutionary Mexico that looks to the future, redeemed from previous historical oppressions. This case study offers an example, perhaps even a constitutive one, of how this traditional element entered the technological and mediatical -as well as the cultural and political- vanguard of Mexico, while also reaching international audiences, triggering transnational relations that would fuel these mortuary national symbols.

title: A Place at the Party: Serving up Generic Hybridity in Fifteenth-century Iberia
summary: This article examines a short eclectic work, Criança y virtuosa dotrina , which dates to the end of the fifteenth century. This work illustrates the rich experimentation with genres that characterizes literary production among graduates of the University of Salamanca, combining a mythological fantasy romance with a courtesy manual that describes the duties and responsibilities of servers at court. This analysis situates the work within the lens of converso literary productions in this charged decade leading up to the Expulsion and argues that this text imagines a covert pathway for fellow conversos to avoid discrimination and assimilate into elite circles. By emphasizing the role of service and highlighting instead the special (and typically invisible) role that servers have played in Iberian court society, the work subtly offers a privileged glimpse into questions of concern in contemporary society and illuminates generic hybridity as a tool to cloak authorial intention. This article ...

title: The Perils of Manipulative Living: Biblical and Theological Perspective
summary: Manipulative living, characterized by deceit, coercion, and the misuse of influence, poses a significant threat to personal integrity, communal harmony, and authentic Christian discipleship. This paper offers a biblical and theological reflection on the dangers of such a lifestyle, demonstrating how Scripture consistently condemns manipulation as antithetical to God’s nature of truth and love. Beginning with Old Testament narratives, where figures such as Jacob and Jezebel reveal the destructive outcomes of manipulation, the study highlights how manipulative actions fracture relationships, undermine justice, and invite divine judgment. In the New Testament, the teachings of Jesus and the writings of the apostles emphasize transparency, humility, and service as marks of true discipleship, directly contrasting with manipulative tendencies rooted in selfish ambition and pride. Theologically, manipulation is exposed as a distortion of human freedom and an abuse of God-given power meant for...

title: Introduction
authors: Jacob M. Dakon, Benjamin D. McWhorter
summary: History informs practice. In his book, What the Best College Teachers Do , Ken Bain notes that the most successful educators have an “unusually keen sense of the histories of their disciplines, including the controversies that have swirled within them,” and that “understanding seems to help them reflect deeply on the nature of thinking within their fields.” 1 Here, Bain touches upon a crucial point within contemporary American string music education. In our never-ending search for the newest best practices, we must start with a thorough examination of our past to best determine our future.

title: How to Make a Film about Radical Environmentalism
summary: Daniel Goldhaber&s;s invocation of Kelly Reichardt&s;s Night Moves (2013) in an interview for his most recent film, How to Blow Up a Pipeline (2022), prompts comparative analysis, and it is this chapter&s;s overarching contention that such analysis can clear ground for a critical discussion of the limits and affordances of narrative cinema vis-à-vis environmental justice. The films make a provocative pairing, no doubt because they feature acts of ecoterrorism but also, and more importantly, because their stylistic dimensions and political messaging are divergent. This chapter contends that ‘modernist exhaustion’ is an apt way of characterising the relationship between these two films. Modernist exhaustion names Goldhaber&s;s impulse to eschew the techniques associated with a cohort of modernist filmmakers, the Italian neorealists, whose work is often where genealogies of contemporary slow cinema begin. title: Migration and the Logic of Reverse Mission
summary: The rejection of ‘metatheology’ and an accompanying hostility toward the term mission within the very subject of missiology resonates with what has been described as the postmodern rejection of metanarratives. The influence of this intellectual climate on understandings of mission is evident in the widespread appropriation of Thomas Kuhn’s theory of paradigm shifts in a plethora of missiological texts. Despite this, non-Western cultures are shaped by distinct indigenous epistemologies, creating tensions when migrant Christians bring very different understandings of truth into Western contexts and churches. This raises important questions for the idea of ‘reverse mission’ advanced by Jehu Hanciles. In this essay, the concept of reverse mission will be re-examined. Focusing on Akan Christian migrants from Ghana ministering in Britain, this article uses an epistemological particularist framework in order to explore how their theological knowledge might be conveyed within a cultural settin...

title: Petroglyphs as petrofacts? Exploring the visibility and physicality of lines, furrows, and cavities in Bronze Age rock art
summary: Abstract This text concerns tangible and sensory aspects of petroglyph production with a primary focus on south Scandinavian Bronze Age rock art. The core of the study is based on an experimental trial of making a cupmark, a circle motif, and a shallow boat motif on a small granite outcrop. The aims were to measure time expenditure, the impact of water on the process, evaluate sensory aspects (e.g. colour, sound, and smell), and measure the visibility of the petroglyphs over time. The direct results of the experiment show that a cupmark can be produced within 12 minutes and a circle within an hour, using a direct technique with a small pointed hammerstone. The shallow boat motif took only seven minutes to make and was almost as visible (white) as the deeper circle motif, even without leaving any measurable depressions in the rock. The results of the present study are related to other published trials concerning Bronze Age rock art. This paper concludes that petroglyphs are probably les...

title: From Sculpture to Porcelain Funeral Photography: Symbolism, Collective Memory, and Public Space
summary: This article explores the evolution of media as instruments of collective memory and symbolic presence, focusing on the historical and technological transition from monumental funerary sculpture to porcelain photography. Through an interdisciplinary approach that combines memory with art history and media theory, the article analyses how changes in materials and memory reflect transformations in the social perception of death, mourning, and immortality. Taking as a case study example from the global context throughout the centuries, but also the Albanian one during the 20th and 21st centuries, the article argues that photography on porcelain democratized visual memory, shifting the focus from the glorification of elite status through sculpture, towards the preservation of individual identity and family intimacy. summary: Abstract The essay departs from the so-called »end of theory« and relates it to transformations of temporal horizons: the loss of an emphatic conception of the future, ecological crises, and artificial intelligence. It engages in conversation with two developments, each starting from the past of (literary) theory: first, the demand for a return to the object of study; second, the historicization of formerly emphatic theory, which is now regarded as a cultural event of former generations. The essay proposes to connect these various directions in a productive way: the literary studies division of labor between theory, method, and object is interpreted temporally with reference to proposals by, among others, the theoreticians of science Mary Hesse and Niklas Luhmann. The role of the object is to represent the constructed past of scientific arguments. Method secures the future in an operative sense: it generates probable possibilities for continuation. title: The Personal Is Political
summary: This chapter sets out to explore the intersection of Third Cinema and Latin American documentary, reframing the discussion through the lenses of Accented cinema and first-person narratives. Departing from conventional norms, it delves into a rich tapestry of voices that have historically been marginalised. The focus is on how Latin American filmmakers utilise accented storytelling and first-person perspectives to disrupt established norms, ultimately redefining the aesthetics of documentary filmmaking. Drawing on Hamid Naficy&s;s concept of Accented cinema, which accentuates the cultural and linguistic distinctiveness of the storyteller, this chapter seeks to explore a filmmaking approach that incorporates unique narrative styles and perspectives rooted in the filmmaker&s;s experiences of displacement and nuanced understandings of ‘home’ and cultural identity.

title: "All I do on this app is cry" : death, grief, and memorialisation content on TikTok
summary: This dissertation examines death, grief, and memorialisation content on TikTok. Drawing on Michael Hviid Jacobsen’s theory of spectacular death as a diagnostic framework and Luciano Floridi’s information ethics as an evaluative framework, the study analyses a corpus of 132 TikTok items collected between April 2024 and January 2025 through purposive sampling. The analysis employs visual analysis, content analysis, and thematic analysis, supplemented by examination of comment sections as sites of collective negotiation around death, grief, and memorialisation content. Organised through three of Jacobsen’s dimensions of spectacular death (mediatisation, re-ritualisation, and commercialisation), the findings demonstrate that these dimensions are structurally inseparable on TikTok: a single piece of content simultaneously participates in all three. The dissertation theorises four conditions that characterise this convergence: death scrolling (the frictionless, algorithmically mediated encou...

title: The “United” Kingdom—Comedy and Satire of the Countries
summary: Abstract The distinct histories and political and cultural traditions of the countries comprising the United Kingdom strongly affected the kinds of comic and satiric periodicals they produced, as well as the humorous and critical content printed in its more general papers. In Wales, Swansea and Cardiff were homes to such papers. Often allied with universities, Scotland’s publishing centers had produced comic publications for many decades, but the last third of the nineteenth century represents a flood, with Glasgow’s The Bailie “My Conscience!,” The Quiz, and The Chiel, Aberdeen’s Bon-Accord, and The Piper ’o Dundee among the most durable, and many other short-lived attempts in Edinburgh. In Ireland, Zoz, its successor Zozimus, and Pat, all strongly nationalist in content, were accomplished comic papers in the manner of Punch, and Ulster had many British patriotic periodicals rise and fall.

summary: The year 2024 marked the fiftieth anniversary of Jacques Rivette’s Céline et Julie vont en bateau/Céline and Julie Go Boating (1974), a delightful odyssey about two women playing dress-up, roller-skating, eating bonbons and drifting in and out of a boudoir melodrama. The film’s mercurial spirit and whimsicality have inspired a diverse range of interpretations. However, as Robin Wood observed, often readings of the film, and readings of Rivette’s films in general, are somewhat narratively impressionistic and leave one with the sense that the narratives are arbitrary. Though plenty of scholarship on the film expresses the opposite, elegantly accounting for narrative details through compelling and varied approaches (through psychoanalytic or feminist optics, for example), Wood’s observation is intriguing. title: Broadway to Main Street
summary: Abstract The crossroads where the music of Broadway met popular culture was an expansive and pervasive juncture throughout most of the twentieth century and continues to influence the cultural discourse of today. Broadway to Main Street: How Show Music Enchanted America details how Americans heard the music from Broadway on every Main Street across the country over the last 125 years, from sheet music, radio, and recordings to television and the Internet. The original Broadway cast album—from the 78 rpm recording of Oklahoma! to the digital download of Hamilton—is one of the most successful, yet undervalued, genres in the history of popular recording. The phenomenon of how show tunes penetrated the American consciousness came not only from the original cast albums but from interpreters such as Frank Sinatra and Barbra Streisand, impresarios such as Rudy Vallee and Ed Sullivan, and record producers such as Jack Kapp and Goddard Lieberson. summary: This chapter examines Sam Dastyari&s;s political memoir One Halal of a Story (2017) as a critique of Australian multiculturalism&s;s promises and failures. Drawing on Ghassan Hage&s;s theories of white multiculturalism and Pierre Bourdieu&s;s concept of cultural capital, the analysis traces the Dastyari family&s;s migration from Iran to Sydney in the 1980s and their struggle for belonging. Despite championing multicultural ideals, the Australian urban landscape presented significant hurdles that insidiously prompted assimilation rather than integration. The chapter argues that multiculturalism operates not as an innocuous policy but as a commodified asset designed to generate surplus value, subject to constant surveillance and regulation by a white managerial gaze. Furthermore, spatial distribution across Australian cities reveals inequalities where class often outweighs racial identity in defining one&s;s spatial domain. title: Not Assimilation, Not Resistance: Proculturation as a Reframe for Autistic Experience Across Nested Cultural Spheres
summary: This conceptual paper reframes autistic experience through Gamsakhurdia's proculturation theory, treating culture as a dynamic, continuously negotiated process rather than a static inheritance. It identifies a threefold impasse in existing frameworks: Berry's acculturation model assumes static cultures and a keep-or-leave binary; deficit and celebration framings in autism research both flatten autistic people into monoliths; and diagnostic norms operate as unexamined cultural artifacts of a settler, WEIRD, and neuronormative context. Against these, the paper introduces the Nested Spheres Model, a cartography of proculturation locating disability not in the person but in the friction between the ontological core, micro-sphere, meso-sphere, and macro-culture. The model reframes masking as a spectrum of semiotic activity, recenters intersectional realities, and reconceives thriving as authored engagement with cultural contact. title: Afición y nación: el cine inédito de Enrique Uribe White
authors: Juan Ferro Reyes, Gabriel Ferro Serrano, Antonia Hollmann
summary: This article offers an analysis of the cinematic production of Enrique Uribe White, whose recent recovery allows him to be positioned as a newly recognized author within the history of Colombian cinema. Based on a biographical review and an examination of his earlier visual practices—photography and the editorial design of PAN magazine—the article argues that his filmic work constitutes a project defined by technical rigor, formal experimentation, and an aesthetic sensibility informed by art history. His films, produced between 1940 and 1959, articulate a representation of the nation marked by tensions between tradition and modernity and by the deliberate use of mise-en-scène.

title: Design as Improvement an Architectural Approach to Lookouts
summary: This essay looks at fire lookouts as a design problem, drawing on two semesters of studio teaching. Unlike the ranger stations the Forest Service built with real architectural care from its earliest days, lookouts were mostly built without any architect involved. The essay argues that a lookout is less a single, unified building than a loose assembly of parts, each with its own history, closer in spirit to folk carpentry and hands-on tinkering than to formal architecture. Rather than treating that improvisation as charming but shapeless, the essay reframes it as "improvement": a steady, ongoing process where each new fix builds on the last instead of replacing it, the way an old building keeps absorbing changes without ever being torn down and started over. The essay ends by arguing that respecting this layered, patched-together logic—not erasing it—is what lets new architectural work stay true to a lookout's history.

title: A Sense of Place, Trauma, and Fantasy in Saeed Fassaei's Rising from the Shadows
summary: This chapter examines Saeed Fassaei&s;s memoir Rising from the Shadows: Revolution, War and the Journey that Made Me (2015) as a study of the relationship between immigration, trauma, and sense of place. Drawing on Edward Relph&s;s phenomenology of place and Jacques Lacan&s;s psychoanalytic concepts of anxiety, desire, and the imaginary order, the analysis explores why Fassaei experiences debilitating PTSD symptoms – including recurring nightmares of his friend Darius&s;s death during the Iran-Iraq war – after migrating to Australia, despite his genuine gratitude and positive attitude toward his new home. The chapter argues that Fassaei&s;s mental distress stems from the dissonance between the fantasised, idealised image of Australia he constructed as a “vicarious insider” in Iran and his actual experiences of cultural disorientation, professional demotion, and occasional racism in the “real” Australia. title: Arte y cine: lazos de familia
summary: The article traces some key moments in the shared history of art and cinema with the aim of highlighting the most significant points of their convergence and mutual influence, which it identifies in citation, the use and adaptation of formats, and, finally, the significance of montage. The text uses both local and international examples to illustrate situations that help build a panoramic perspective. The purpose of this reflection is to demonstrate that the dialogue between art and cinema —far from being easy and peaceful or reflecting an established hierarchy— reveals, instead, a constant conflict in the struggle to captivate audiences, carve out spaces, and establish a place within the context.

title: Face/Off
authors: Katharine Sarikakis, Angeliki Chatziefraimidou, Gentiana Ramadani, Simon Haslauer, Mariia Yeroshkina
summary: This chapter explores cinema as a site of social justice and a tool for unveiling and addressing pressing equality challenges. These two dimensions are inextricably connected, as the diversity of voices brought into the production process reflects social injustice and is mirrored in the cinematic product. Focusing on the concept of meritocracy and societal inequality, the study delves into the intricate ways in which film serves as a platform for social engagement and a catalyst for change. Crucial to our exploration is an examination of the diversity of voices behind these cinematic narratives and the channels through which these stories are disseminated. The study uses interviews, documents, policy analysis, and state-of-the-art methods to address these social inequalities in cinema.

title: Losing My Timing This Late in My Career
summary: Abstract By the early 1970s, Broadway music would be branded “middle of the road,” but the expressway of popular music left little, if any, room for the show music for an earlier or current generation. Various new teams and new songwriters attempted a cross-generational sound, a way of bringing rock-infused scores to Broadway: Burt Bacharach and Hal David, John Barry, Stephen Schwartz, and Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice. Not all of their experiments were successful—either on the pop charts or on stage. Stephen Sondheim emerged as the preeminent composer/lyricist of his generation and, in the midst of commercial failure within the world of cast albums, Sondheim emerged with a hit song that eventually became a pop standard in an increasingly obstreperous time: “Send in the Clowns,” introduced as a crossover single by Frank Sinatra.

summary: A remembered event can retain real information without being a replay of the original experience. This possibility changes what a memory experiment must explain. title: The political economy of halal certification regulation in the Philippines: religious-class fractions, local and global arenas, and state transformation
summary: As the global halal economy continues to expand, many countries are increasingly confronting the policy challenges surrounding halal certification. While halal exportation operates within the neoliberal framework of free trade, its regulation is governed by fragmented regulatory arrangements engineered by rival networks of halal certification bodies (HCBs) which hamper seamless cross-border flows of halal-certified goods. Such arrangements have impacts on domestic regulation for HCBs. This thesis examines one case, the Philippines, where efforts to participate in the lucrative global halal market have been complicated by the existence of multiple and competing regulatory regimes governing HCBs. In one regulatory arrangement, state bodies accredit HCBs, while in another, HCBs pursue private self-regulation. This raises an important question: why do contradictory regulatory regimes for HCBs coexist within a single regulatory territory?

title: “We Know How to Navigate This Place, and You Won't”
authors: Helen Lomax, Kate Smith, Maria Jesus Alfaro-Simmonds
summary: Our chapter responds to Wendy Luttrell’s (2010 , reproduced in this volume) influential paper and provocation to visual scholars to carefully consider their ethical responsibilities to children as co-creators of visual research. It offers reflections on what images made with children “do” in the process of their digital circulation and how an ethical stance that is responsive to children’s expertise, care, and visual literacy can offer more equitable forms of ethical decision-making. Drawing on an example of young people’s zine-making as part of participatory research exploring their experiences of growing up in socio-economically disadvantaged neighborhoods, the chapter foregrounds children’s expertise, care, and visual literacy, capabilities that they draw upon to make ethical decisions about how to curate and share their visual research. title: The Independent Artist
summary: The continued growth of independent, self-managed artists is improving to the point that they now account for 47 percent of the global music industry, based on ownership ( Whitt 2024 ). Independent artists and labels generated over US$14.3 billion in 2023. Growth for this sector of the global music industry occurred during one of the first rebound years following the global pandemic.

title: The Construction of Embodied Habitus in Dance Creation Based on Women's Dual Roles as a Production of Bodily Knowledge: A Literature Review
authors: Lydia Devi Nursanthi, I Wayan Dana, Hendro Martono
summary: This research aims to examine the construction of embodied habitus in the creation of dance as the production of bodily knowledge through a synthesis of literature on embodiment, habitus, dance practice, and women's agency. The method used is a conceptual qualitative literature review of international journal articles relevant to the theme of the body as a medium for the formation of identity, social experience, and cultural meaning. Data are collected through identification, selection, in-depth reading, and thematic categorization to identify patterns of relationships among concepts. The results of the study show that the body in dance practice functions as an epistemological medium that integrates cognitive, emotional, social, and cultural dimensions. Habitus is formed through the repetition of bodily experiences that result in a disposition of actions and reinforce the transmission of cultural values. In addition, women are represented as cultural agents and creative subjects who pl...

title: Introduction
summary: This chapter invites readers to follow the author&s;s initial observations and foundational work that shaped the creation of this book. It provides an overview of what smartphone communities are and how they will be explored throughout, including a brief section on methodology and the book&s;s structure. The central argument posits that smartphone communities are fluid, evolving formations of society, constantly in a state of becoming. Processes of community formation and dissolution become momentarily observable through digital traces – status updates, location sharing, image galleries, contact lists, and other artefacts from various apps and platforms. Employing praxeological and discourse-analytical methods, the book examines the dynamics of community-building at the intersection of smartphone technology, discursive frameworks, and user practices.

title: Sharpening bordering: What counts, where it operates, and what endures
summary: We respond to Laine's account of supply chains as bordering infrastructures by asking three linked questions: What counts as bordering, where does it operate, and what forms endure? We argue that bordering: (1) depends on identifiable mechanisms that differentially organize mobility; (2) operates at the intersection of territorial authority and networked infrastructure; and (3) may leave capacities that outlast particular practices. This argument extends to the post-pandemic era, where bordering capacities are strategically hardening under geopolitical, economic, and environmental instability.

title: The Horizontal Dimension
summary: Voice leading—how chords are created by the motion of individual voices—is one of the main concerns of conventional tonal theory. 1 Even today, the voice-leading conventions followed by composers of the tonal era occupy an important part of the course of study in colleges and universities around the world. But a glance at the table of contents of this book will reveal that voice-leading conventions are not a central issue in post-tonal music. In fact, as we will see later in this chapter, one of the most hallowed principles of voice leading was an early casualty of the assault on musical conventions made by a number of composers around the beginning of the twentieth century.

title: Japanese imperial nationalism in the classroom
summary: This chapter explores how Japanese imperial nationalism was advanced through colonial education in Korea by analysing eight Japanese language textbooks for elementary schools, issued under the First to Fourth Joseon Education Ordinances. Utilising critical discourse analysis and visual image analysis, the study examines how these textbooks operated as instruments of imperial ideology and control. Koreans were systematically portrayed as passive, obedient, and industrious, ideal traits for loyal colonial subjects, thus legitimising Japanese domination and encouraging assimilation. The curriculum prioritised the Japanese language and cultural norms to reshape Korean identity in line with the Empire’s political and ideological goals. Over time, the focus in the textbooks shifted from loyalty to labour and eventually to full assimilation, mirroring Japan’s changing colonial strategies and wartime mobilisation efforts. title: Fractured Frames and Fearful Fictions
summary: This study examines the rhetorical landscape shaped by Tucker Carlson during his peak as host of Fox News’ highest-rated show, anchoring the analysis within sociological debates on media polarization and political identity. Carlson’s program functioned not just as news, but as a platform for cultural performance—reinforcing conservative identity and sharpening divisions with strategic emotional appeal. Through a combination of paranoia, moral panic, and populist grievance, Carlson advanced narratives that cast certain institutions and individuals—particularly those tied to child welfare and COVID-19 medical policy—as threats to national integrity. These frames weren&s;t incidental; they were part of a deliberate effort to trigger fear and fortify in-group loyalty. Rather than fostering public debate, Carlson’s rhetoric contributed to an alternative informational world—what some scholars call the conservative counter-sphere. Within this space, misinformation doesn&s;t merely confuse; it...

title: Lessons in Artist Management
summary: Chapter 5 is a series of mini-case studies about artists and managers, all of whom can offer insight into the artist–management relationship. Artists who are featured in this chapter include Chance the Rapper, Elvis Presley, Michael Jackson, Eminem, Garth Brooks, The Backstreet Boys, The Rolling Stones, Kesha, and Kelly Clarkson.

summary: The year 2022 marked the 10th anniversary of the course Critical Animal Studies: Animals in Society, Culture and the Media at the Department of Communication and Media at Lund University. title: Serialism after 1945
summary: The end of World War II in 1945 was followed by two major developments in music. One of these was the beginnings of electronic music, the subject of Chapter 12. The other development, the subject of this chapter, was the dissemination of the serial technique and the extension of its principles into all facets of musical composition.

title: From Underground to Primetime
summary: Drag as a performance art has long occupied a unique and sometimes precarious position within popular culture. From its playful reconfiguration of gender norms to its brazen disregard for binaries, drag has long functioned as a site of subversion. In the late 20th century, scholars and cultural critics celebrated drag as an art form that unsettled gender categories and resisted normative constraints on how bodies should look and behave. J. Brian Brown’s 2000 article “Doing Drag: A Visual Case Study for Gender Performance” is a key work that captures this essence. Drawing on life-history interviews and field observations, Brown emphasizes how drag simultaneously compounds and challenges hegemonic masculinity. However, as drag has increasingly moved into the mainstream over the past decade, buoyed by television shows such as RuPaul’s Drag Race , a central question persists: can drag still disrupt entrenched gender codes, or has commodification diluted its subversive potential? Moreover, ...

title: Conclusion
summary: This chapter concludes by reflecting on the enduring nature of smartphone communities in a rapidly evolving technological landscape. It highlights how smartphone connectivity fosters both private and public, virtual and physical communities, shaped by participation, resistance, and technology. Through a temporal lens, it emphasizes how smartphones synchronize human and technical time, facilitating constant interaction. The fluidity of these communities mirrors the evolving nature of social interactions, underscoring the paradox of hyper-connectivity, which both unites and polarizes. Ultimately, smartphone communities embody a dynamic process of continuous reformation, leaving a lasting imprint on modern communication, social behaviour, and collective practices.

title: Bonds and the individual's odyssey in the group
authors: Di Moisè S. Scappaticci Anne Lise
summary: This text describes the odyssey of the infant in search of himself within the tension between belonging to a group and developing individuality. Emotional bonds are presented as fundamental to the formation of thought, linking the processes of containing and being contained. Knowledge arises from emotional experience, in which love, hatred and envy play central roles. Faith is understood as the capacity to sustain hope in the absence of sensory certainty and to maintain contact with psychic reality. The work explores how these emotional bonds shape the relationship between the individual and both internal and external groups. Through an autobiographical reflection on analytic training, the author narrates a personal journey that also represents the path of every analyst. Myths are used as models to illuminate the dynamics between individual and group, highlighting the primordial foundations of the mind and the human search for meaning and belonging.

summary: This article takes Soft Power , David Henry Hwang’s “musical within a play”, to foreground the importance of transnational appreciation in an era of superpowers. The article identifies Hwang’s strategy as “reciprocal criticism” – utilizing other cultures for self-critique without establishing superiority but rather encouraging mutual improvement – and highlighting performativity: it does not merely describe issues but creates a new reality through the re-imagining of The King and I , an orientalist musical, into a contemporary piece of theatre that elevates Asian American voices. summary: Dating apps have become central to contemporary digital leisure, functioning as immersive environments where intimacy, pleasure, and safety are negotiated across digital and embodied contexts. Drawing on feminist theory, post-humanist perspectives, and narrative inquiry, this study examines how these platformed leisure spaces shape sexual objectification, safety, and agency. Interviews with 48 diverse Canadian users reveal a complex leisurescape shaped by image-centred design, rapid sexualization, and emotional and safety labour, particularly for women and gender-diverse participants. Users navigate spaces where pleasure and harm coexist, requiring vigilance, boundary-setting, and resistance. Practices such as blocking, reporting, and strategic self-presentation demonstrate meaningful but constrained agency shaped by platform affordances, gendered norms, and broader systems of power. title: Minimalism and Beyond
summary: This chapter is concerned with minimalism and with other trends that came to the fore even later. These later trends are known by an array of labels such as postminimalism, the new romanticism, the new tonality, totalism, eclecticism, and polystylistics. All of these categories, which are for the most part fuzzily defined and overlapping, share at least one characteristic with each other as well as with minimalism: to some extent, at least, the music that they represent is pitch-centric and occasionally even tonal in the traditional sense of the term.

title: The Last Stage
summary: This essay examines the Austrian reception of Wanda Jakubowska’s 1948 film Ostatni etap (The Last Stage). Set in Auschwitz, it was one of the earliest feature films to depict the Nazi concentration camp system. Drawing on contemporary newspaper reviews and press coverage, it traces the film’s path to theatrical release in Vienna and beyond. While some commentators emphasized the film’s importance as an act of remembrance and antifascist testimony, others reframed it through anticommunist comparisons to Soviet camps. In this way, the Austrian reception of The Last Stage reflects broader patterns of postwar memory politics in early Austrian public discourse.

title: Queer Interventions, Now and Then
summary: This essay explores the dynamic nature of queerness and its representation in visual studies, highlighting how cultural conditions shape our understanding of queer identities. Through an analysis on works produced by Brown’s “Doing Drag” and Mulder and Scheele’s “If Males Were Photographed Like Females”, I emphasize that these essays served as radical interventions against gender essentialism while also reflecting their contexts’ limitations. By treating these texts as living archives, I argue for the importance of revisiting queer material studies to foster understanding and encourage resilience in the face of ongoing societal challenges. This chapter was written in collective response to reprinted archival essays by Katrin Mulder and Emmy Scheele (1983) and J. Brian Brown (2001) for the subsection of The Visual Studies Companion , “Doing Reciprocity”, which features an introduction by Alpesh Kantilal Patel and essays by Gillian Yee, Erin Riley-Lopez, Vee Forsell, and Martina Merlo.

It analyses Thích Nhất Hạnh&s;s critique of later concentration-centred systems and his insistence on mindfulness as an integrated practice involving body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. The chapter further examines Zen as a mode of direct realization rather than a sectarian identity, highlighting poetry, calligraphy, and ordinary actions as extensions of meditation. Practices such as mindful walking, gāthā recitation, reconciliation rituals, and communal living are analysed as sites where insight matures into compassion. title: The Man and His Heirs
summary: Pierce Egan made his contemporary reputation not in literature, but on the remote fringes of it, although, as so often happens with practitioners of popular or sub-literary forms, he was to be a not insignificant influence on literature that came after him. His proper milieu is the world of journalism and the popular theatre; his concern was not with writing enduring works, but with recording the activities of those in the lower strata of society and revealing the unknown London and Londoners. He is an excellent reporter, not only of sports, in which he excels, but of people at their amusements, of crime and criminals, of Londoners individually and in the mass, and of any aspect of life and fashion that takes his particular attention.

title: No Tire, No Movement
authors: David Garbin, Simon Coleman, Andrew Esiebo, Inês Valle
summary: Drawing on the Pneuma-City project, this chapter brings together ethnography and photography to examine tire repair, waste, and material circulation as central dimensions of urban life in Lagos, Nigeria. Framed through the motto of Lagos’s tire repairers, “No tire, no movement,” tires are analyzed as forms of frictional infrastructure that mediate mobility, labor, and urban inequality. The project follows the multiple afterlives of rubber, from hazardous street waste to improvised infrastructure, leisure objects, and upcycled artworks that traverse social and spatial boundaries. Through techniques of framing and the use of slow shutter speed to register tensions between immobility and movement, some of these images situate tires within broader urban rhythms. The essay concludes by reflecting on the notion of pneuma —air as both invisible and material—to highlight how care, repair, and undervalued labor keep the megacity in motion.

Specifically, it identifies three dimensions of its reward: (1) elaborating on Montaigne’s discussion of the challenge we face when acknowledging the possibility of unexpected death, it maintains that Socratic insight into one’s mortality can promote one’s pleasure in life and increases the experience of freedom; (2) reconstructing Spinoza’s doctrine of the amor Dei intellectualis, it argues that self-knowledge can increase our self-acceptance and make us appreciate the constitutive goodness of being; (3) engaging with Rousseau’s late writings, it suggests that reflection on our inner life enables people to focus on their sentiment about their own existence and helps them transform their amour propre into a mature self-love. title: The Artist Prepares to Be Managed
summary: This chapter offers a guide to artists who are ready to move their careers to “the next level” with detailed points to ensure they are ready. It has the artist do some detailed introspection about who they are artistically, along with the reality that they are planning to move into the business side of the music industry. The chapter ends with a list of questions the artist should ask a prospective manager as well as questions an artist can expect from a prospective manager, with notes about why each question is being asked.

title: Conversation with Ji Yoon Yang
authors: Ji Yoon Yang, Kate Korroch, Julie Patarin-Jossec
summary: In this conversation, curator and director of Alternative Space LOOP, Ji Yoon Yang, discusses her multifaceted approach to curatorial work while currently leading the first alternative art space in Seoul, South Korea (Korea hereafter). In conversation with co-editors Julie Patarin-Jossec and Kate Korroch, Yang discusses her career path, the history of Alternative Space LOOP and how LOOP is situated in the South Korean art scene. Yang leads projects through hands on feminist curatorial practice that expands beyond traditional spaces, and moves into the realm of anti-capitalist ecofeminist strategies. The interview ends with advice for visual sociologists who endeavor to have a curatorial practice. The transcript was edited for clarity and length.

title: Reverb, Chillwave, and the Disinterested Hipster
summary: Abstract This article examines the role of reverb in shaping the sonic and cultural identity of chillwave, a genre that emerged in the late 2000s and became emblematic of the disinterested hipster aesthetic. Focusing on the production techniques in tracks by Washed Out and other early chillwave artists, it explores how reverb acts as both a genre-defining timbral feature and a semiotic cue for affective distance. By drawing on sound studies, music theory, and affect theory, the article argues that reverb creates a hazy, emotionally detached vocal presence that aligns with the ironic, cultivated apathy of the disinterested hipster figure. The analysis traces this connection through the cultural moment of Portlandia ’s 2011 premiere and tracks the aesthetic evolution of the disinterested hipster in American pop culture. Additionally, the article considers how reverb, while often associated with detachment in chillwave, can also signify emotional dissociation, trauma, or vulnerability in ...

summary: Contemporary Buddhism, Mindfulness and Thích Nhất Hạnh’s Teachings explores mindfulness and the modernization of the Buddhist mind through the teaching of Zen Master Thích Nhất Hạnh, inviting readers to rediscover Buddhism as a living tradition. The book seeks to make the Dharma relevant, accessible and practical for the contemporary world. Through a textual study of Thích Nhất Hạnh’s writings, it investigates his understanding of the nature of interbeing, the nature of mind and the application of mindfulness and Dharma as practical tools for self-transformation. It situates Nhất Hạnh’s work within classical Buddhist sources, highlighting how principles of mindful practice can transcend cultural boundaries and be globally relevant while remaining rooted in the essence of Buddhist teaching. The book demonstrates how Buddhist thought can evolve to meet modern challenges without losing its spiritual depth and how Nhất Hạnh’s work demonstrates contemplative practice grounded in lived under...

title: The Aesthetics of the Burok Dance Performance in Cirebon: An Analysis of Symbolic Aesthetics and Performance Aesthetics
summary: The Burok Dance is a traditional Cirebon art form that developed among the coastal communities of West Java. This art form combines elements of dance, music, parades, religious symbols, and folk entertainment in one form of cultural performance. This study aims to assess the aesthetics of the Burok Dance performance through symbolic aesthetics and performance aesthetics. The research method used is descriptive qualitative with a literature review. The results indicate that the aesthetics of the Burok Dance lie not only in the visual form of the performance, but also in the symbolic meaning, social values, and collective experiences of the supporting community. The elements of color, movement, costume, music, and figurative form of the Burok represent a blend of Islamic, local Cirebon, and popular culture that shape the distinctive aesthetic identity of the coastal community. Thus, the Burok Dance represents a folk aesthetic that is dynamic, communicative, and rich in cultural meaning.

title: Landscapes of Hybrid Activism
summary: The year 2022 marked the 10th anniversary of the course Critical Animal Studies: Animals in Society, Culture and the Media at the Department of Communication and Media at Lund University. As the first initiative of its kind in Sweden, the course explores the shifting roles and positions of non-human animals in today’s complex societies. It aims to equip students with analytical tools to critically assess norms and structures that organise human-animal relations, along with their ethical, cultural, and social consequences. What started as a one-course offering driven by an idea has evolved into a decade-long project of education and emancipation for non- human animals. This anthology stands as a testament to the course’s impact, aiming to extend the rich discussions, debates, and insights cultivated beyond the classroom walls. title: “They found only anguish where there should have been joy”
summary: Through the lens of a case study, this chapter examines marriage dissolution and the intersections between secular and ecclesiastical authorities and personal, familial, and societal expectations. Marriage has long been a key institution: it represented far more than a bond between two individuals, shaping status, property, lineage, and family strategy more than romantic attachment. Within this context, the Church played a significant role, asserting and maintaining its power over minds by seeking to control bodies. As this chapter shows, the body emerges as a crucial site through which power was exercised. This is exemplified in the understanding of consummation as possessing a “founding power,” whereas the non-consummation of marriage was seen as disrupting the “societal order.” Drawing on various primary sources, including archival documents, legal journals, and collections of acts and laws, and by reconstructing the various stages of the litigation between a husband and wife from S...

title: Life in Ireland
summary: For the next five years Egan, having seen the writing on the wall only too plainly, was virtually to abandon sporting writing for the theatre. He was clearly at this time at a low financial ebb, and, now almost sixty, would doubtless have been delighted to have found a permanent niche somewhere. But, although he bombarded managers with proposals, outlines and scripts for plays, burlettas, pantomimes and ‘comic operas’, almost all of them proved to be as unexcited at the prospect of presenting an Egan stage masterpiece as Elliston had been. One factor in his lack of success was undoubtedly that to which he referred in his letter to Elliston—his being labelled as a ‘slang writer’ and a portrayer of low life, and the difficulty managers found in considering him in any other role. Some were more sympathetic than Elliston, however, to the man, if not to his work.

title: Disability and ableism
summary: This chapter considers the term ‘disability’ and the meaning associated with it. It explores invisible disabilities and the terminology that the reader chooses to use. The concept of ableism is discussed, as well as internalized ableism.

title: Colonial Influence, Opium Trade, and Romantic Imagination: A Postcolonial Reading of Thomas De Quincey’s “Confessions of an English Opium-Eater
summary: Background: Romantic literary scholarship has increasingly examined the relationship between Romantic imagination and British imperial expansion, yet the material role of colonial commodities in shaping metropolitan consciousness remains comparatively underexplored. Thomas De Quincey’s Confessions of an English Opium-Eater provides a significant site for examining this relationship because its account of addiction, memory, reverie, and altered consciousness is closely connected to opium as a globally circulated colonial commodity. Purpose: This study examines how colonial commerce, opium consumption, Orientalist representation, and Romantic imagination intersect in De Quincey’s Confessions. It specifically explores how imperial structures enter metropolitan consciousness through commodities, urban space, racialized representation, and imaginative experience. title: Hong Kong echoes across English ghost lands: A decolonizing of English-language poetry
summary: This article focuses on three women poets who deploy a Hong Kong Chinese imaginary, an imaginarium filled with memories, popular cultural references, fragments of Cantonese, and isolated Chinese characters. Jennifer Lee Tsai was born in the UK of Hong Kong immigrant parents, while Jennifer Wong migrated from Hong Kong to the UK first to study and then to write poetry. Tim Tim Cheng similarly migrated to the UK to study, having grown up in Hong Kong. Their English-language poems are peppered with Cantonese images and linguistic elements that challenge the reader to address the postcolonial condition of the poetry. Written in English in the UK, their poetry represents a poïesis of the local and the personal. While articulating a local everydayness, their work seeks out from afar and from the past, in the migrant in-betweenness of Chinese–British borderlands, poetic resolutions to the binds of their postcolonial subjecthood.

title: Grand Masters and the Grand Tour
summary: This chapter examines the Masonic dimensions of the Grand Tour in late eighteenth-century Sicily. While studies of the Grand Tour have traditionally emphasized the attraction of Italian art, antiquities, landscapes, and classical ruins, this chapter argues that Sicilian travel also unfolded through dense networks of sociability, recommendation, hospitality, and intellectual exchange shaped in part by Freemasonry. Focusing on French travelers such as Dominique Vivant Denon, Déodat de Dolomieu, and Jean-Pierre Houël, the chapter traces their encounters with Sicilian aristocrats, collectors, naturalists, and antiquarians, including the princes of Biscari, Palagonia, and Torremuzza, Saverio Landolina, Giuseppe Gioeni, and other local figures connected to Masonic circles. title: It Must Have Been Love (But It's Over Now): Thematic Changes in Popular U.S. Song Lyrics Across 4+ Decades
authors: Janet B. Ruscher, Katherine B. Carnelley
summary: Over time, U.S. marriage rates have decreased, as people increasingly expect romantic relationships to satisfy high-level needs. Concurrently, interest in sexualized relationships (e.g., hook-ups; consensual nonmonogamy) has increased. Reflecting these patterns over time, song lyrics may become less about prototypical romantic love and more about noncommitted sexual relationships. Using the Meaning Extraction module in LIWC-22, four independent content themes were pulled from the top 25 songs of the Billboard Hot 100 from 1980 to 2024 ( N = 1,129). Themes were correlated with chart year and LIWC linguistic categories. Lyrics high on a Fall in (or out of) Love theme (content words like love, heart, break ) became less common and used past and future tense. In contrast, lyrics high on a Contact theme (e.g., talk, stop, call) became more common, more sexualized (sexual and swear words), and avoided future tense. title: Conclusions
summary: We have called our book Young Readers Responding to Poems to indicate that ‘response’ is a process not a product, or even a series of products. Readers come to terms with poems over time; and, with those poems we come to feel are worth reading, the process remains open-ended; we never finish with such poems. The tremor of unease English teachers often feel when they hear themselves say that they have ‘done’ this or that poem with a class signals the mismatch between the process of reading and responding and what usually happens to poems within the constraints of the classroom where the stress is usually upon pinning the meaning down. In fact, we know that meaning cannot be fixed; that poems — like paintings or sculptures — are infinitely renewable; and that in good poems we will discover fresh things each time we read them and enjoy being reminded of old things.

title: A Fine-Grained Image Dataset of Gold and Silver Artifacts from the Tomb of Prince Liangzhuang and Preliminary LoRA-Based Generation Experiments
authors: Yelei Chen, Yifan Xu, Lei Shu, Ru Han
summary: The digital preservation of cultural heritage is evolving from static archiving towards intelligent creation. As representative examples of early Ming Dynasty gold and silver craftsmanship, the gold and silver artifacts from the Tomb of Prince Liangzhuang, with their complex craftsmanship and rich cultural significance embodied in their decorative motifs, pose substantial challenges for digital preservation and innovative design. Generative artificial intelligence currently faces difficulties in reproducing fine-grained forms and decorative features, while the lack of high-quality, multi-dimensionally annotated image data specifically designed for such artifacts further constrains their digital preservation and application. To address these issues, this study constructed a fine-grained, multi-dimensional annotated image dataset of gold and silver artifacts from the Tomb of Prince Liangzhuang. authors: Katrien Tiidenberg, Asko Lehmuskallio, Maria Schreiber
summary: This chapter explores the changing landscape of visuality in the age of social media, offering a conceptual framework grounded in the notions of cuts and configurations to analyze shifts in visual practices, technologies, and discourses. Rather than focusing on transient trends or platforms, the chapter advocates for an approach that attends to both continuity and transformation in visual culture. Through layered analyses of practices (e.g., looking, seeing, and showing), technological shifts (e.g., the smartphone camera, algorithms), and discursive formations (e.g., platform governance, visual ideologies), the chapter’s framework reveals social media visuality as both a site of innovation and enduring patterns. title: Form in Post-Tonal Music
summary: All of the formal structures and procedures found in the tonal era survived in post-tonal music. That is, in post-tonal music we still encounter sonatas and rondos, canons and fugues, sectional and continuous variations, and binary and ternary forms. Not surprisingly, many works employing traditional formal structures date from the first few decades of the twentieth century or were composed by relatively conservative composers, but this is not always the case. For instance, Schoenberg, hardly considered by his contemporaries to be a conservative, often composed in classical forms.

title: High-school stories and semiotic bodies: autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) in the cultural field
summary: Abstract In dialogue with Sigmund Freud, D. W. Winnicott, Stuart Hall and Julia Kristeva, this article examines ASMR as phenomena, representational form and modality of performance. Through a close analysis of the high-school subgenre, it is argued that affect and storytelling are interlaced, re-presenting the ASMRtist as actor and performer, and demonstrating the interdependence of semiotic and symbolic dimensions of content. Themed videos presenting the ‘toxic best friend’ and the ‘girl who is obsessed with you’ (re)inscribe sensuality on feminine bodies, producing a form of ‘killjoy’ queering irreducible to a specific sexual identity. The subgenre creates a reiterative scene in which adolescent experience is traced on the body as sensory, sensual, and intimate.

Questions are asked regarding the nature of design-led artefactual journeys – and the use of walking interviews – to better expose entrepreneurial design heuristics. summary: Descent dressing is a cardinal aspect of culture and religions globally to enhance dignity and safeguard one from molestation as well as command respect. The hijab derived from the Arabic root h-j-h may meaning to cover or shield symbolizes a spiritual bond between Muslim women and God to live a life of decency and self-respect. It is a significant aspect of Islamic religious practice and Muslim women's identity, particularly in relation to modesty, faith, dignity, morality, and social belonging. Rooted in Islamic teachings concerning modesty and decency, hijab is widely understood as an outward expression of religious commitment and obedience to God. However, its significance extends beyond physical appearance to include values such as chastity, humility, self discipline, dignity, responsible behaviour, and spiritual consciousness.
